That is not the way we should be supporting our young people. It does not allow them to grow or establish the full lives that we all want them to have. It also deeply damages that social contract with the wider public, because if an increasing number of people feel that the system no longer adequately distributes wealth and does not represent the importance of paying in and supporting those who belong in it, we will find that there will be a growing resentment—not against those who are unable to work, but against those who can work but choose not to do so. That fundamentally damages the reciprocity of the social contract of this country.

May life grant me the confidence, conviction, and lack of shame of a Conservative MP who is enraged by problems that they either helped to create or did nothing about when they had the chance. I do not think there has been a Conservative Government in my lifetime who have not said that they would cut welfare spending, and then attempted to blame their failure to do so on the sick, the poor and the young, and what we hear from the Opposition today is the same old approach, which would lead to the same old failures from the same old Tories. I am old enough to remember when George Osborne promised us a high-wage, low-tax, low-welfare country. Instead, we saw child poverty skyrocket, food banks open in every community, young people written off, and a welfare bill that went up by a record £33 billion in the Conservatives’ last year in power alone. Opposition Members cannot be trusted to fix the welfare system, because they are unwilling to be honest about how the money would be spent, or to simply address the question of why people need support. They know full well that most of the welfare bill is spent on pensions, and that in the future, to protect pensions, decisions will have to be taken, such as on whether to adjust the triple lock. Instead, what we get from the Opposition is a bogus petition designed to stoke fear and division, proposals to push children back into poverty, and an open attack on the working poor. The Opposition’s proposals fail to acknowledge that 3.1 million people receiving universal credit this year are in work, that one in five working-age people receiving personal independence payments are in employment, and that 58% of households helped by the removal of the two-child benefit cap have at least one parent in work. If we are genuinely to reduce dependency on welfare, we must tackle the things that make people need that support in the first place: low pay, poor health, the cost of housing and, perhaps most importantly, child poverty. As research from the Joseph Rowntree Foundation shows, young people who experience persistent childhood poverty are 3.4 times more likely to be out of education and employment by the time they turn 23. That should concern every Member of this House, because poverty does not simply disappear when a child turns 18; it can shape their education, health and opportunities for the rest of their life. If we fail to address those barriers today, we risk creating greater costs for our welfare system tomorrow. The sad thing is that everyone in this House agrees that the system can and should be fixed, because a system that spends £1 on support for every £25 on benefits is not right. Is it time to do this differently, and to work across the House to design a system that is about lifting people up, instead of writing them off? I am proud that this Labour Government have removed the two-child benefit cap and lifted half a million children out of poverty. I welcome the £3.5 billion investment in employment support for the sick and disabled. Reducing welfare dependency cannot simply mean reducing the support that people need; it should mean reducing the need for that support in the first place, and that cannot be achieved by the same old approach that leads to the same old failures from the same old Tories.

It is heartbreaking that we still have a such a large proportion of working poor in our society, and that so many people across my constituency, and the constituencies of others Members, are working hard, making sacrifices and doing their best, yet are still being punished by increasingly oppressive policies that take one look at the reality of hardship faced by folk, and decide to look the other way. One thing that is clear, and has always been clear, is that we cannot cut our way to prosperity—the Tories’ own record shows that to be true. The way to get the welfare bill down is not to arbitrarily pick targets and experiment with people’s lives to score political points, and it is genuinely insulting that Conservative Members can come here today and try to offer half-baked solutions to problems that they created. This is largely a problem of the Conservative party’s own making. Conservative Members are trying to blame those in our society who rely on support because they cannot accept responsibility for their own actions. We must make it clear how misguided at best, or intentionally reckless at worst, the Conservative party is when it comes to welfare, because its austerity-fuelled cuts were linked directly to rising levels of poverty, and they have exacerbated the overall cost, long term. Anyone minded to listen to the Conservative party on their arbitrary welfare targets might need to seriously check themselves. Of course we do not want people to rely on welfare long term, but there is a trend over past years—largely instigated by Conservative Members, but it is increasingly found wider afield—to blame those who rely on additional support for Government mismanagement, instead of recognising that many who receive such support are already valuable, contributing members of our society. This trend completely fails to address why so many working-age, motivated and skilled individuals still have no choice but to rely on additional support. Indeed, many people are able to contribute to our society and economy only because they receive additional support. Rather than blame those people, there must be more intense scrutiny of why so many people have to rely on that support, why so many are dependent on universal credit despite being in full-time employment, and why so many young people are relying on jobseeker’s allowance. It is not because they do not want to work and are not looking for work; it is because the Labour Government have priced them out of employment by creating such a hostile hiring environment. So many parents and families rely on the Scottish child payment because life is just so unaffordable. I am especially concerned about young people who are coming of age today. A young person in my constituency who graduated from a university in England or Wales might have over £60,000 of debt, which they will likely be paying off for their entire life, and that amount will rise year on year because of interest. They have started paying that debt back earlier because Labour refused to amend the threshold freeze. A young person might not be able to find a job because the employer national insurance contribution hike is pricing young people out of work, or because of the refusal to cut VAT on hospitality, or because of the total mismanagement of minimum wage reforms. A young person could be paying more than £1,000 in energy bills; they are due to rise again in January, because of Labour’s choices. A young person who cannot afford to save knows that they will likely never buy a house, might never receive a state pension, and faces unaffordable monthly living costs. As one of the youngest Members in this House, it is so frustrating to come here and hear others speaking about the reality for young people without actually understanding what they are facing, and to see the discrepancy between apparent support from the Government and the reality for young people in my constituency. Yes, I want the welfare bill to come down, but the way

I start by disappointing Conservative Members: I agree with some of what they are saying. The welfare bill is too high, and too many young people are not in education, employment or training; it is morally indefensible. The problem is that Conservative Members seem to have forgotten who was in charge when those trends first took hold. In their final year in office, the welfare bill rose by a record £33 billion. Listening to some of the speeches this afternoon, one might think that Conservative Members had spent 14 years campaigning against Conservative Governments. They are right to highlight the growing number of young people who are not in education, employment or training, but it is not a new problem. It did not begin last year, or in July 2024; it grew on their watch, and yes, it has continued since. Frankly, that should prompt some humility, not self-righteousness from Conservative Members. I also agree with Conservative Members when they say that we need to spend much more on defence. What puzzles me, however, is the argument that all we need to do is cut welfare, and the defence budget will somehow take care of itself. If it is that easy, why did they not do it? They had 14 years in government, and over those 14 years, welfare spending rose while, in the words of a former Defence Secretary, our armed forces were “hollowed out”. What exactly are Conservative Members asking us to learn from their example—that it is entirely possible to end up with a growing welfare bill and shrinking military capability at the same time? Anyone on the Opposition Benches can demand cuts, but it is the responsibility of the Government to ensure that reform actually works. Earlier this year, I brought together a group of young people from my constituency who were not in education, employment or training. Not one of them told me that welfare was the reason that they were out of work. They talked about poor or non-existent careers advice; artificial intelligence and the rapidly changing labour market; and struggling to get employers to give them a chance, because they lacked confidence or soft skills, in some cases. In other words, they talked about barriers. We can ignore those barriers and make speeches about random, crude cuts to welfare, or we can try to deal with them. I would much rather do the latter. Real welfare reform is not measured by how much money leaves the Treasury; it is measured by how many people can enter and remain in work. The Opposition are right to demand welfare reform and stronger defence, but they have no right to pretend that they bear no responsibility for the position in which this country finds itself on either score. After their 14 years in government, the welfare bill had risen and our military was hollowed out. The country needs welfare reform and stronger defence, but demanding change is not the same as delivering it. The real test is whether more people find work, whether barriers are removed, and whether our armed forces are genuinely stronger. None of those challenges will be solved by that lot on the Opposition Benches pretending that the previous 14 years did not happen.

I have a solemn duty to talk about an incredibly difficult and challenging statistic in relation to the prosperity of this country: the size and scale of worklessness in our country right now. Some 6.7 million working-age people are claiming benefits and are not in work. That is one in six of our working-age population. I do not know how anyone can hear that statistic and not be horrified by what it represents for the prosperity of a country that seeks to do well. Historically, that figure has been around one in 10. It causes me particular concern, for a number of reasons, that today’s figure is related to an increase in claims for mental health challenges and disabilities. We have talked about the challenges of ensuring that people do not feel stigmatised or labelled in a way that will not be conducive to their finding work. When it comes to mental health conditions such as depression, we have to recognise that getting in work and getting a job is advantageous to someone’s mental health, and that not working is a disadvantage to their mental health. I am afraid that there is also the challenge of fraud in the benefits system. We all have to accept that the benign view of human nature that we have heard expressed by Government Members, in which no one is ever induced or encouraged to make a claim that might not reflect their reality, is naive in the extreme.

Let me finish my point. The fact is that mental health conditions are almost entirely self-reported. People are asked questions that relate to how they feel, what their mood is and what they can or cannot do, and we must accept that that inevitably has a risk of inducing or encouraging people to exaggerate their claims. The hon. Member for Ealing Southall (Deirdre Costigan) is not in her place any more, but she inadvertently accepted that point when she talked about the disability living allowance, and how the changes that were made encouraged people to put in higher claims. That in itself is admitting that people say or do different things depending on the available incentives. We must not forget that a welfare system does not exist in isolation; it is part of a wider society. All of us face a complex mixture of incentives and disincentives to do the right thing. There will be people at either end of the spectrum, but a lot of people are at a point in between. That is why I support our policies, which make it very clear that when it comes to access to cash, being on benefits is not the same thing as being in work, and it should not be the same thing. I support our plans to make the welfare state more about helping and supporting people with the things that they need, rather than just giving them money. That is also why I support our plans on the two-child benefit cap. We should never create a situation in which people who are working have to make tough decisions that those on benefits are excluded from having to make. Government Members like to say that benefits are claimed by people in work, which is true, but the claimant numbers do not reflect how the money is spent. More than 80% of the money spent is spent on people who are not in work. A much smaller proportion of expenditure is on people who are in work. That is why I support the idea that the system should have two tracks: a track for people who have put into the system, who can then fairly ask more of it when they are in need, versus a track for people who have never put into the system. These are the incentives and disincentives that we all interact with in society. When I meet and speak to people on the frontline who work with people who are in poverty and claiming the support of charities and other sectors, they are very clear about that. They will freely talk about the people who come to see them—the people who they think are legitimate and really in need, and the people who they think are not. That is why I find it so extraordinary that Government Members never seem to want to acknowledge what we all know is a real pressure in society.

We heard from the hon. Member for Torbay (Steve Darling) that 20 or 30 years ago, a person born with a brain injury would be unlikely to survive. Today, such people survive and live with a disability for the rest of their life—people like my daughter. Is the hon. Member for Bexhill and Battle (Dr Mullan) really saying that because those people have never paid in or contributed, they are not entitled to any help from the state?

That is not the system that we propose. We are talking about people who have had an opportunity to contribute and have not done so; the system should take that into account. That is a fair and reasonable point to make.
The hon. Member is talking about contributions and people who have contributed. Does that include foreign nationals?

I do not think that foreign nationals should be entitled to benefits, because of the basis on which they are allowed into our country. The only reason they are allowed into our country is that they are net contributors. Why would we undermine that by allowing them to be net recipients of benefits? They are only here because they have signed up to the idea that they will come and be net contributors, so I do not think that that entitles them.

Just so that I am clear, if somebody is born in another country, comes here and gets citizenship or indefinite leave to remain, and has contributed to the system because they have been working, should they be able to claim from the system? That was my question. They may well have been a high earner, but they may have fallen on hard times and fallen back on the system that we all rely on, and they may have contributed to that system.

They are citizens, are they not? They have signed a deeper contract with the country that they are in, and they are here under a different set of circumstances. The hon. Member needs to be clearer when she asks her questions in relation to two different groups of people, because we treat them very differently in our proposals. There is a distinction. Let me make a final point that is often not talked about enough. We are all incredibly focused on what the Government should do to help people and how taxpayers should help people. We know that for very many people in poverty, a big factor in that is having absent parents who give them absolutely no money or pitiful amounts of money for very many years. We also know that a large proportion of families with children who are in absolute poverty would not be in poverty if an absent parent who is not paying was paying. I wish that there was as much focus on the dereliction of duty that parents too often show to their children and the complete failure for decades to tackle that issue, across all parties, as there is on what taxpayers and the state should deliver. That is a significant moral failing that we are too shy to talk about in this country, and it does not get the attention that it needs. If all parents, whether they have split up or are together, contributed to the upkeep of their children, we would see a lot less child poverty; I wish that MPs on all sides of the House were as invested in that issue as they are in deciding how much the state should pay in their place.

Let me start on that last point. I am the proud son of a single mother, and I am probably standing here today only because of the support that she got from the last Labour Government. There are three things that we as Members can agree on. First, the welfare bill is too high, and the trajectory is unsustainable. Spending on disability benefits alone has risen from £45 billion last year and is forecast to reach almost £70 billion by 2031-32. If we want to protect the welfare state, we must make it more sustainable. Secondly, we have a duty to protect those who cannot work and provide a safety net for those who work but have fallen on hard times. That is what the welfare state is for. Thirdly, helping more people into work is good not only for the Treasury, but, as many people have said, for those individuals. Good work brings dignity, purpose, independence and often better health. That matters, because this debate is presented as a contrast between those who are willing to reform the welfare system and those who want the status quo, but I reject that. I believe in reforming the welfare state because I am a Labour politician, not despite it. The disagreement is on how we do that and the determination with which we push through changes. We have seen that just announcing spending cuts does not achieve them. The Conservatives announced £11 billion of welfare cuts in 2010. In 2015, they promised another £12 billion. When they introduced PIP, they expected it to reduce spending by 20% compared with the system that it replaced; instead, the OBR said that it increased spending. Even before the pandemic, working-age disability benefits spending was rising by more than 5% a year in real terms. Announcing savings does not always lead to delivering them. There are two reasons for that, both of which are relevant to the Opposition’s proposals. First, cutting one benefit can simply move the cost elsewhere. Take local housing allowance; the Opposition have announced that they are going to add extra limits to that, as well as reinstate the two-child benefit limit. Imagine a family with three young children who are already struggling to pay the rent. They could lose support for their third child while their housing allowance is pegged to a level that covers only the cheapest tenth of local properties. What happens is that they can now no longer afford their home. Quite rightly, I think there is consensus across the Chamber that we do not leave children sleeping on the pavement, and I do not believe the Opposition are arguing against that.

The hon. Gentleman is talking about local housing allowance. The Prime Minister said that he felt a freeze in local housing allowance was simply a cost-shunt on to local authorities, but the Chancellor went ahead and did it anyway. Does the hon. Gentleman think the Chancellor was right, or was the Prime Minister right to criticise him?

I sit on the Housing, Communities and Local Government Committee, and we have discussed raising LHA a lot. However, the Conservatives’ proposal goes even further, and would ultimately have a real effect on the temporary housing bill. Last year, councils in England spent £2.9 billion on temporary accommodation. In London, the number of homeless children in such accommodation is equivalent to at least one in every classroom—if you cut in one place, it whacks the cost up somewhere else. That is before we get on to the wider costs, including disrupting schooling, parents being forced out of work, and pressure on the NHS. Most horrifically of all, in the six years since 2019, 104 children died with temporary accommodation recorded as contributing to their vulnerability, ill health or death. Seventy-six of those children were under the age of one. We all accept that policies involve trade-offs, but that is probably one that we should all find pretty difficult to stomach. For the Conservatives to put forward such a policy without even having modelled its impact on temporary accommodation and wider impact on the welfare bill, shows that those proposals have not been well thought through. Yes, we need to come up with sustainable ways to address the welfare bill. We will see more from the reviews that are coming forward, and I will be proud to support them.

From 2010 to 2024, every reform was opposed and every initiative was rebuffed by people who sat on the Opposition Benches. Labour Members remind me of St Augustine, because they try to tell us that they are now serious about welfare reform. Their prayer is “Make me a welfare reformer, but not yet”, because when they had the opportunity to introduce some reform, they rebelled. Keir Starmer blinked, the rebels got their way, and the reform agenda was kiboshed. The Prime Minister lost his authority, and the rest, as they say, is history. Do not take my word for it; the current Secretary of State for Work and Pensions told the whole world. He said that “Every meeting I have” with Labour MPs—not some, not the majority, but every meeting— “is ‘Who can we tax in order to pay benefits to others?’”.

Going back to the speech made by my right hon. Friend the Member for Witham (Priti Patel), when she was the Minister of State for Employment, I was her Parliamentary Private Secretary. We would sit through many a Westminster Hall debate secured by the Opposition, who are now the Government, complaining that we just were not spending enough. They said about every reform we brought forward, “Not good enough. You need to spend more.” There was never any attempt to reduce the welfare bill.

My right hon. Friend is right. As I said in an intervention on the hon. Member for Wirral West (Matthew Patrick), the Government had 14 years to plan for this great reform and modernisation of welfare, and they did nothing with it. They arrive in government, and precious little happens.
Is the hon. Gentleman’s position seriously that it is Labour’s fault that the welfare bill went up under the Conservatives?

No, that would be an asinine interpretation of what I have just said. The point I am making is that every time the Conservative party came up with a reform or a modernisation when in government, the gut reaction of the Labour party was to oppose it. I happen to think that the welfare state is one of our crowning glories. It was brought in to address a number of deeply systemic societal problems, and it has been a tremendous force for good and transformation in our country. However, it is always intended to be a safety net, a permanent safety net for those who—as a result of disability, for example—find themselves unable to enter the workplace. It removes pressure and anxiety, and it gives people the dignity to live that they quite legitimately deserve, but it should never have been allowed under successive Administrations to become a cocoon. It has ceased to be a safety net; it has become a trap with perverse, Kafkaesque incentives, where the cumulative benefits an individual can receive are greater than anything they could hope to aspire to when getting into a job for the first time. I hope the House can agree that there is nothing kind or caring about trapping people in that sort of environment. We all know—as various right hon. and hon. Members have mentioned in their speech—the fundamental importance and transformative nature of work for individuals, their families and their communities. It promotes a sense of self-respect, self-reliance, and being able to do things for yourself.

I will not. The benefits of work are clear and unquestionable, yet we are trapping people through perverse incentives; if they earn an extra pound here or there, they suddenly lose a great slew of benefits. Surely—I say this to Members on the Treasury Bench—we will have to be far more imaginative and far more bespoke in how we approach welfare. We should be using digital and the raft of opportunities it offers to provide a far more bespoke, personally tailored network of support to get people back into work, rather than trapping them. I want to say one thing about disability, as I had the honour of chairing the all-party parliamentary group for multiple sclerosis in the last Parliament. We will get more disabled people back into work because they want to stay in work—for all the reasons I have set out—if they have the confidence that they can ask their employer for reasonable adjustments, and if their employer has the confidence to ask what the employee might need in order to stay in work. Let us not have a slanging match across the two Dispatch Boxes; let us try to work cross-party. It will be good for the economy and good for our people up and down the land, and it will generate greater tax receipts to pay for the social services, defence and other areas that we want to see expenditure in. However, the status quo cannot be defended.

What we should be talking about in this debate is root-and-branch reform of our welfare system, providing more opportunities for work for those who can work while protecting those who cannot. We should be talking about innovation and investment in employability to tackle the scourge of youth unemployment in our communities. What we should not have is the weaponisation of this debate and point scoring by a party whose record on this issue does not stand up to the slightest scrutiny. On the Conservatives’ watch, spending on incapacity and disability benefits for working-age adults rose by £20 billion between 2019 and 2024, while progress on closing the disability employment gap stalled. When they left office, nearly 900,000 young people were not in education, employment or training and the disability employment gap stood at nearly 30%. The legacy in my constituency is that Fife has the fourth-lowest rate of 16 to 19-year-olds in education, training or work of Scotland’s 32 council areas. In Buckhaven and Methil in my constituency, one in eight of those aged 16 to 19 is a NEET, putting the area among the five worst wards in the whole of Scotland. It is not rocket science to work out how that happened. We had a Conservative Government at Westminster failing to take the action required to provide more opportunities for our young people and to close the disability employment gap. Regrettably, we had an SNP Scottish Government cutting budgets for skills and training. I hope that Scottish Ministers will respond positively to the Prime Minister’s invitation to work with the UK Government to devolve powers and resources on employment to Scotland’s regions, as we are doing in England and Wales. Importantly, this Government are not waiting for the final conclusions of the Milburn review, but are instead heeding the important call for change made in his interim report. We have the youth guarantee, backed by £1.5 billion of funding. We are introducing the youth jobs grant to incentivise employers to hire young people who have been on universal credit for six months. The Secretary of State recently had the opportunity to visit the youth hub in the constituency of my hon. Friend the Member for West Dunbartonshire (Douglas McAllister). Young people who had never worked before are already finding jobs as a result of the support they are receiving from the youth hub. There is plenty of evidence of what works with employability support. The community trade hub in Buckhaven in my constituency is reaching young people who were non-attenders at school, but are now getting the skills they need for the work of the future. The brilliant Enable Works scheme, where I used to work, is bringing third sector organisations together with expertise in employability. Could the work of the third sector make an even greater contribution with this vital change for disabled people, for young people and for our country?

No welfare system stands the test of time in perpetuity. Loopholes appear in all well-intentioned systems. People test the system, and the world does not stand still. That is why the last Conservative Government came into office with a plan to tackle the welfare bill that had ballooned under Labour, and they did tackle welfare. The right hon. Member for East Ham (Sir Stephen Timms) asked earlier in this debate, “In which years under the last Conservative Government did the welfare bill come down?” I am happy to be able to assist him. Under the last Conservative Government, the working welfare bill came down in 2012. It came down in 2013. It came down in 2014. It came down in 2015. It came down in 2016. It came down in 2017. It came down in 2018. It came down in 2019. Between 2010 and 2019, the working welfare bill came down by a fifth. That is the legacy of the last Conservative Government’s reforms. I live in the real world, and I accept that covid changed everything. It changed the relationship between the individual and the state. From that time, the welfare bill started to climb. Those were the conditions that Labour knew it would have to deal with as it came into government, and it failed to deliver. Labour did not even have a plan to tackle the welfare bill, which it knew had been climbing year on year since covid. At least the last Prime Minister, Keir Starmer, cobbled together some form of plan. It was a pretty rubbish plan, but a year and a half ago he tried to get some crude cuts through the House of only £5 billion-worth of savings. He failed, though, because the same MPs sitting opposite me now on the Government Benches stopped him. The current Prime Minister came into office a few months ago and flirted with the idea of bringing down the welfare bill, but he has given up entirely and he is proud of it. He is so proud that he will not bring the welfare bill down that he has ruled it out for the remainder of this Parliament. The right hon. Member for East Ham has been tasked with finding savings, and he is about to publish his review into PIP. We know what will be in that review when it comes to savings: absolutely nothing, because the Prime Minister has already ruled it out. The Labour party is the welfare party. Its Members are proud of welfare spending going up and up. Just a few hours ago, at the Dispatch Box, the Prime Minister criticised our party’s plan to save £36 billion because it will hit incomes during a cost of living crisis. The system of benefits and personal independence payments is not intended to be an income top-up. It is not even means-tested. It is there to help people with a genuine need to meet the daily cost of a disability. I am afraid that the Prime Minister’s mask has slipped if he thinks it is there to serve as an income top-up during a cost of living crisis of his own making. Let me now deal with some of the contributions from Labour Members. The hon. Member for Wirral West (Matthew Patrick) brought up the subject of child poverty. The best way to help hard-working families tackle child poverty is to make sure that they have well-paid jobs—to get off the backs of wealth creators, get off the backs of business and reverse the harmful job tax, as my hon. Friend the Member for Bromsgrove (Bradley Thomas) has asked.

The hon. Member has accepted from the Dispatch Box that the Conservatives did completely lose control of the budget, but will he also accept that, contrary to what they keep saying on the airwaves and in the House, the numbers increased more between spring 2022 and spring 2024 than they did between spring 2020 and spring 2022? Moreover, covid was not the cause; the cause was the fact that, at the back end of their Government, they lost control of the economy, they lost control of our borders, they lost control of the SEND system, and they lost control of DWP budgets.

I fundamentally disagree with the hon. Member’s claim that covid and its legacy had no effect. I think he should go back and think again about what life was like during covid and in the aftermath. I turn now to our plan. We will not make the mistake that the Labour party made in opposition. We will not sit by and let a system become more and more unfair without doing the hard graft. As my hon. Friend the Member for Solihull West and Shirley (Dr Shastri-Hurst) pointed out, it is not fair to leave the system as it is. Our plan includes £36.1 billion of welfare savings to help get Britain working. Ensuring support for people with genuine need is at the heart of it, and we will provide £1 billion for people with lower-level mental health conditions. That is new money to help them and ensure that we can make savings of £16.5 billion by removing them from the cash handout system, giving them the therapeutic support that they need instead.

My time is short, so let me finish by addressing the critics head-on: those who say that we do not understand—that we do not understand mental health, and that I do not understand what it is like to live with a neurodevelopmental disorder. Well, I do know what it is like. I have an ADHD diagnosis, but I have never been told that I cannot do something, and I have never been told that I need more help to do it. My condition was undiagnosed for 30 years. People with ADHD do not need a disabled persons railcard, they do not need a Motability car, and most of them do not need a cash payment every month to meet the cost of a disability for ADHD alone. The Government need to stop thinking of new ways to give more people more things. Instead, we need to ensure that people have access to therapeutic community support to help them to live, learn, train, work, and get on in life. That is good for the economy, it is good for society and, most of all, it is good for the individuals involved. That is not the Labour way; it is the Conservative way.

Given that time is short, I hope that my hon. Friends will forgive me for not being able to respond at length and reflect on the excellent contributions that we have heard. However, I want to thank my hon. Friend the Member for Gloucester (Alex McIntyre)—whom, of course, I will meet, as he requested—and my hon. Friends the Members for Wirral West (Matthew Patrick), for Ealing Southall (Deirdre Costigan), for Bexleyheath and Crayford (Daniel Francis), for Croydon East (Natasha Irons), for Banbury (Sean Woodcock), for Milton Keynes North (Chris Curtis) and for Glenrothes and Mid Fife (Richard Baker) for their passionate speeches. In particular, I want to highlight the contribution of my hon. Friend the Member for Gedling (Michael Payne), whose demolition job on the Opposition’s proposals was truly something to behold. In her opening speech, the shadow Secretary of State suggested that it was a little early for the panto season. However, people could be forgiven for their confusion, given that the Tories have rushed out their Christmas wish list of cuts somewhat early this year. Before turning to those particular proposals, however, I want to comment on some of the other points made by the shadow Secretary of State. We agree that the number of unemployed young people is unacceptable. The number of young people not in education, employment or training was, of course, up by 250,000 in their final three years in office. We commissioned the Milburn review, the youth guarantee and the youth jobs grant because we are determined to right their wrong. The hon. Lady said that reforming welfare is not cruel. Again, I agree with her, but the Conservatives’ plans are not welfare reform; they are cruel cuts. She said that we cancelled their reforms, but it is worth remembering that their 2023 consultation on reforming the work capability assessment was ruled unlawful. Let us turn to some of the specific proposals in the plans that the hon. Lady spoke to, which would push hundreds of thousands of children into poverty. Half a million young people would be impacted by the Conservatives’ proposal to reinstate the two-child limit, with well over half the children affected in families that are in work. The Child Poverty Action Group has said that the Tories’ measures, including the reinstatement of the two-child limit, would cause “the biggest overnight increase in child poverty since records began.” It is absolutely shameful. The Conservatives’ changes to housing benefit would exacerbate homelessness and add costs. They have proposed to reduce local housing allowance to the 10th percentile of local rent, instead of the current 30th percentile. Expert organisations have said that this would dramatically increase homelessness, as well as displacing costs to local authorities, the NHS and other public services. The director of the Chartered Institute of Housing says: “At a time when record numbers of households are already struggling with housing costs, this would almost certainly increase financial hardship and homelessness. Any short-term savings to the welfare bill could quickly be outweighed by higher costs to councils, the NHS and other public services”.
I am grateful to the Minister for giving way on welfare bill savings. Can he confirm that the Labour party’s 10-year plan will contain detailed plans for reducing the bill?

As the hon. Gentleman is aware, we have been clear that we will set out our proposals for welfare reform next year. They will be scored by the OBR in the usual way. Turning back to the Conservatives’ proposed changes to local housing allowance, I have already quoted the Chartered Institute of Housing. I rather prefer the slightly snappier comments of the chief executive of Shelter, who said: “Making more families homeless does not save the government money.” It is not rocket science, but it needs explaining to some Members of this House. The Conservatives have not said what would happen to British people, including children in households that contain foreign nationals. They have not set out how a household with a foreign national and a British citizen partner would be treated. Universal credit is, of course, a household benefit. Would that household be treated as a single person claim, instead of a couple claim? Would the household lose all eligibility? What about households containing foreign national adults living with British citizen children? Would the Tories’ policy on foreign nationals hit the income and living standards of British people? From the information available to us at present, it certainly seems that that would be the case. Let us turn to the laughably ambitious £13.7 billion that the Conservatives claim they can save by reforming disability and sickness benefit. They say that this would be achieved by introducing more detailed and holistic assessments with tighter eligibility criteria, but the current contracts, which they signed us up to, run until 2029. They say that they can deliver all this by 2030, yet those contracts include a target for face-to-face assessments of just 20%. It is undeliverable. Of course, that is before one considers that the Conservatives’ costings are predicated on claimants’ primary condition only. The shadow Secretary of State quoted the IFS, which has been very clear that most people in the cohorts that the Conservative party hopes to take benefits away from actually have multiple conditions, and often three or four. The Tories have no idea what those people’s conditions are, so the numbers are just total fantasy. Overall, they refuse to say how many households or individuals would lose out. The hon. Member for Ruislip, Northwood and Pinner (David Simmonds) said that the Conservatives were protecting pensioners. That is not the case, because the transition from PIP to attendance allowance that they will force on people reaching pension age could cost somebody up to £4,160 a year. That would be someone on the higher rate of PIP for both daily living and mobility moving on to the higher rate of attendance allowance, so it could in some cases be more. I suspect that the Conservatives do not know how many people would be affected, I suspect they do not have a precise figure for how much it will save, and I fully expect—now I have pointed out that they are not, in fact, protecting pensioners—that that proposal will disappear, because many of these things do not stand up to scrutiny. The challenge with the proposals the Conservatives have put forward is that they are not worth the paper they are written on. A serious Opposition would have done their homework properly, but what do we have instead? They claim to have a plan for welfare that works, but who exactly does it work for? Not for the children plunged into poverty, not for the taxpayers who have to foot the cost, not for the pensioners who face a £4,000 cliff edge and not for the households facing homelessness. We know how punitive policies turn out: more hardship, less opportunity and more pressure on the welfare state. This Government will not repeat the Conservatives’ mistakes. We are fixing the broken welfare system they left in their wake, and ensuring that everyone gets the support they need so that they can fulfil their potential and truly have a better future. Question put (Standing Order No. 31(2)), That the original word
I inform the House that Mr Speaker has not selected the amendment. I call the shadow Secretary of State.

I beg to move, That this House believes that employers are working people and therefore condemns the Government for breaking the Labour Party manifesto commitment not to increase National Insurance by increasing employers’ National Insurance contributions; and calls on the Government to halve employers’ National Insurance contributions for under-25s. Today, we debate a simple proposition: that employers are working people. One might have assumed it a blindingly obvious proposition, but it is one that Labour contorts itself to deny. But, then, Labour is not very good at answering obvious questions, like, “What is a woman?” or “Should someone identifying as a llama be taken seriously?”—remember that one? Yes, the “working people” definition has really been flummoxing Labour Members. For two years, they have been bending themselves into funny shapes. The right hon. Member for Bristol North West (Darren Jones) said that a working person is “anyone that gets a payslip, basically”. The Secretary of State for Transport said that working people were “people on modest incomes”. The Chief Secretary to the Treasury confirmed that employers are not working people. Last week, the First Secretary cleared it all up by saying that working people “do not have savings…and…rely on good public services.” —[ Official Report , 4 November 2026; Vol. 792, c. 910.] That might explain why the Budget hiked taxes on savers. It is a Cirque du Soleil of mental gymnastics—but why? Because in 2024 Labour decided, albeit briefly, that it would rather get elected to govern the country than continue its audition to lead the student union of Islington ring road university, so it made everyone a promise in its manifesto: no tax increases for working people. It got specific: there was to be no VAT hike and no extra rates of income tax, and Labour would not increase national insurance—no way. Just months later, up shoots national insurance to the tune of £25 billion a year. Suddenly, working people across the country are asking, “What the hell happened?”. Labour told working people, “No, no, it’s all perfectly legit—it’s an increase in national insurance for employers, not employees.” I think that is what Labour MPs might normally call gaslighting, but since it is being done to people who contribute, work themselves silly and generally want the country to succeed, their feelings are of no concern to the Government.

I am afraid that I must disagree with my hon. Friend. I do not think the Labour Government were gaslighting the nation. So little is their understanding of business and their ability to read an Office for Budget Responsibility analysis that they did not realise that the nearly £27 billion hit on the nation’s economy would lead to a nearly £20 billion reduction in the money that ordinary people get in their pay packets, and that the net receipt to the Treasury would be about half that—about £10 billion. They cannot add up. Perhaps my hon. Friend needs to acknowledge that they have that disability.

I ask for my right hon. Friend’s forgiveness. I buy into his theory more than mine; I have overestimated the Government’s capabilities. The Conservatives’ motion says that the House believes that employers are working people, and that increasing national insurance broke Labour’s manifesto. If this was just a debate about semantics, maybe we could all move on, but the 2024 Budget has cast a shadow over every employer in every postcode, driving up unemployment and pushing up costs for everyone. It is time to start unravelling that damage, and in particular the damage that this tax increase has done to young people.

For what it is worth, I accept that employers are working people and they are an important part of our labour market and our economy. However, though I lament the increase to national insurance, it was necessary to get money back into the NHS, which was on its knees following the end of the last Government, and that was breaking the economy too.

The hon. Gentleman has no doubt been to his constituency and been denied access to pubs, salons and all the rest of it, and that has suddenly changed his mind about what constitutes “a working person”. I should ask: are his constituents seeing those better public services? Certainly, mine are not, and they wonder where all that money has gone because it has not gone on more stable public finances or better public services. Let us start by acknowledging what it takes to be an employer. It takes someone who saved money to start a business of their own and who took a risk to expand it gradually to take on that first member of staff, then over time building a team. It takes long hours, personal sacrifice, financial peril, time away from their family.

My hon. Friend characterises a picture that might be seen in every constituency among small and medium-sized enterprises. Sometimes, people imagine business as consisting wholly of globalist corporate plutocrats, but the backbone of our economy is made up of those small and medium-sized firms of exactly the kind that she describes. On the issue of public services, why does the Labour party not focus on productivity? It is not wholly about what we spend; it is what we get for what we spend.

I agree with what my right hon. Friend says. That characterisation of employers is why Labour gets itself into such problems in the first place. He talks about the issues relating to national insurance and public services. The NHS also has to pay a higher national insurance bill because of the changes that the Labour Government have made, and that has caused all kinds of challenges across the public sector.

My hon. Friend is exactly right. One of the biggest problems when national insurance went up was that places such as hospices, pharmacies and care homes were not excluded. It is one thing to say that we are putting more money in, but all that money and more was taken elsewhere to pay for the staffing. Is that not part of the problem?

It is absolutely part of the problem. Labour did not think that through, and I have an example of that same phenomenon with the hospice in my constituency, as well as with a number of public sector organisations and charities.

To build on that point, the same applies to the education setting. I met some of my headteachers just last week. Despite employer national insurance going up, central Government grant covers only about 70% of the cost, so the additional 30% must come out of the existing school budget. That has led to teaching assistants being let go and made redundant in my constituency. Does my hon. Friend not agree that that detrimental increase in tax has hit everybody across every constituency?

I completely agree with my hon. Friend. It has been seen in my constituency and across Whitehall. It is an absolute dog’s dinner of a policy that has created problems for not just the private sector but the public sector.

The shadow Minister makes a point about the increases to national insurance—absolutely fine; that is a political point that she is entitled to make. Will she tell me, using the exact same logic that she has applied to the criticism of this levy, why in 2021 she voted for the hypothecated health and social care levy, which was a 1.25% increase on national insurance for both employees and employers? Why was that an acceptable increase, but this was not?

That was a policy that was put forward. My right hon. Friend the Member for Richmond and Northallerton (Rishi Sunak) decided to change it because the economy was in a challenging state after the pandemic and we needed to think again about whether it was the right thing to put that pressure on employers, so we went back on that policy. To return to what employers have been going through, they have the ongoing stress and responsibility of employing people and wanting so desperately to continue to provide opportunity for them. They have to think about the other families who are relying on them as small business founders who are pushing to provide a community with a great service and a happy experience. They are pub landlords, builders, restaurateurs, service firms, salon owners, café owners, shop owners. Work, work, work, work, work. Employers are not just working people; they are uber-taxpayers. They made it through covid, they made it through an energy crisis, but many are now saying that they cannot make it through Labour. When Labour broke its manifesto commitment in its first Budget by increasing national insurance, it did so in a highly destructive way. Not only did it increase the rate, but it lowered the point at which employers start paying NI on an employee’s salary. Lowering that threshold hit part-time, entry-level and lower-wage jobs the hardest, making employees so much more expensive to retain. I do not know about you, Madam Deputy Speaker, but suddenly, countless businesses in my constituency started sounding the alarm, especially those employing people who need flexible, part-time hours because of caring responsibilities.

I thank the shadow Minister for highlighting the impact on part-time workers. My constituency is a very seasonal area on the coast, but we also have students and OAPs, all of whom want part-time work, yet under this Government they are finding that so much harder to achieve.

My hon. Friend is absolutely right to highlight that challenge in seasonal working, which creates an extra burden for employers, many of whom have to work to fill the shifts they would otherwise have used temporary staff for, creating enormous pressure. People are writing to me in despair because their adult child simply cannot get a first break in the workplace, and it is not for want of trying. Businesses warned the Government that this would happen. The hospitality, retail and care sectors all raised the alarm about the impact of higher employer national insurance. What was Labour’s response? The unemployment Act, which makes it riskier to employ people as well as more expensive. The national insurance increase came into effect in April 2025. By April this year, there were 210,000 fewer payrolled employees than a year earlier. There are now 1 million young people not in education, employment or training, and the Government are in denial about the reasons why.

The shadow Minister talks about businesses having warned the Labour Government about the impact that Labour’s jobs tax was going to have. Does she, like me, think it is inconceivable that Treasury officials would not similarly have advised the Government that this would be a consequence of the jobs tax? Is it not particularly pernicious of Labour to have put the biggest barricade in front of younger workers, possibly accessing their first job in hospitality, which will have a lifelong damaging effect on their careers?

The hon. Gentleman is absolutely right to point that out. It is inconceivable that the Government would not have been told about the impact that this policy was likely to have. Labour likes to point out that employers do not pay national insurance on workers under 21, but that misses the point. Employers are making decisions about their entire workforce, and when the cost of employing people rises and the risks associated with taking on a new starter increase, the first opportunity to disappear is the one that will no longer be created. Rather than take on an extra employee at junior level, employers are squeezing the staffing resource they have, but they are shedding younger workers, too. By 2027, employing a full-time minimum wage worker over the age of 21 will cost a business 20% more than it did when Labour entered office. For an 18 to 20-year-old, it is 31%. Labour knows that there is a problem, but rather than tackle it at source, it offers up the youth guarantee, a bung to employers to take on a young person for six months. How about making it cheaper and easier to employ that young person in the first place? Soon we will get details of an unlimited youth mobility scheme with the EU to add to this mix, which will see young Britons competing for available work with peers from 27 other nations. The cost of all this must be absorbed somewhere. Higher national insurance, soaring energy bills and a growing burden of regulation all feed through into the price of doing business and, ultimately, the price we all pay. The weekly shop costs more, a meal out costs more, getting your hair done costs more, activities with the kids cost more, as does going away for a few days. This is just one of the reasons that household finances are going backwards. Whether Labour is talking about employer national insurance or employee national insurance, everybody pays at the end of the day. We Conservatives want more working people, because work is dignity, contribution, resilience and confidence, and we want that opportunity for as many young people as possible. We want to end the waste of a generation unable to showcase its talents, and we want to reduce the cost on a generation of workers that can bear no more tax on its shoulders. That means returning to some of the policies that are driving this destruction. Not only would we repeal the job-destroying provisions of the unemployment Act; we Conservatives would halve employer national insurance for under-25s. Our policy would permanently reduce the cost of employing young people and give businesses a real incentive to take them on. For an employer, it would be a saving of around £1,500. This is part of a wider plan to tackle Labour’s youth jobs emergency. Our “Get to Work” scheme would stop young people leaving education and drifting straight on to welfare. It would create 100,000 new apprenticeships, cut red tape to save the Saturday job and reduce high street business rates to support the businesses that give young people their first step on the jobs ladder—a policy that would benefit not 70,000 high street businesses, as Labour’s policy would, but 250,000. Aside from old prejudices about employers as the oppressors of workers, the reason that Labour contorts itself on the definition of working people is that it knows it has taxed them silly. In doing so, it has not just broken its manifesto commitment but completely undermined what Keir Starmer and his sparkling new Chancellor used to say was Labour’s No. 1 priority: growth. The consequences are there for all to see in the unemployment figures and the living despair of young people unable to secure a good job.

My hon. Friend is making a fundamental point about the structural effects of this policy: of course, it affects profitability year by year, but it also undermines the capacity of businesses to reinvest and ensure structurally that they are fit for the future. A butcher in my constituency, Andrew Parsons of Bennetts Butchers, is closing the shop in a couple of weeks after more than 100 years of trading, because, as a result of the costs lumped on him by successive Governments but particularly by this one, he does not have the money to reinvest.

My right hon. Friend tells us a terrible story that is unfortunately being played out in constituencies across this country. People are having their buffer eroded and then they are simply not able to invest in their businesses in the way that they would have hoped. It was all so predictable. Let me close by reading out what I said to my constituents immediately after the 2024 Budget: “Labour said in the election they did not need to hike taxes to pay for their plans, beyond those they had already announced. We now know this was not true—they have gone on a borrowing and spending spree that makes a mockery of the idea that they are concerned about the state of public finances they inherited. Many of the taxes on ordinary working people have been disguised by heaping pain on business. Labour may think it’s clever politics. But the result will be job losses, higher prices and closures…this approach is all wrong, warping the incentive structure in our economy. It won’t work and as they come back for more taxes, the number of people willing to take the risk of starting a business or save for their families will simply get smaller and smaller.” We are now living that future. Have these tax rises given us robust public finances? Have they delivered better public services? Do people feel better off? On all counts, the answer is no, yet this new Prime Minister believes that the solution to the resulting welfare crisis is to give Labour more taxes to spend. It does not work. Employers are the funders of services, the drivers of growth and the engines of opportunity. Many are not just working people themselves but working people on steroids, and they are fed up of being the cash machine for Labour’s faux benevolence. Their requests are simple: give us the chance to grow our businesses and build a future pipeline of young people to whom one day we might well pass our life’s work. It is time for this Government to start undoing the damage they have wreaked and halve the jobs tax on the young people whose aspirations Labour is burying right now.

The Budget of two weeks ago was a Budget to steer Britain through the economic storms we are facing. It provided breathing space now on the cost of living and the cost of business with fresh hope for the future, and it was built on fiscal discipline, which underwrites every promise this Government make. When the Chancellor stood at this Dispatch Box two weeks ago, he faced a choice: he could have followed the route of the Conservatives—sacrifice stability, borrow irresponsibly and make unfunded promises straight out of Liz Truss’s playbook—but instead he chose a responsible route to keep the public finances under control, protect working people, back businesses and invest in Britain’s future.
I have asked this question a number of times over the past couple of years: could the right hon. Gentleman define “working people” for the House?

Working people are those millions of people across the country who put so much in every day but have not been getting back what they deserve. Those are the people this Government are backing, and that is why, at this Budget, the Chancellor chose to prioritise breathing space for families and businesses, including on the cost of energy. He set out how we will tackle the long-term challenges facing our country. For families, that will mean a £100 household energy payment to support 20 million households—80% of households in England—along with an extension of the VAT cut for electricity bills and a further extension to the fuel duty freeze.

I am grateful for the Minister giving way—I have a huge amount of respect for him. He is always the brave Minister who has to pad up and go out to bat to defend the indefensible, such as the jobs tax, the family farm tax or the family business tax. I wonder if the Minister could enlighten me: if there is a pub landlord hiring local people and serving beer to customers—who may or may not own black Labradors—are they a working person?

Of course they are. If the hon. Member wants to talk about defending the indefensible, I wonder how he ever stands up in this place to talk about the previous Conservative Government because that must be an insurmountable challenge. I hope that he would welcome what the Chancellor announced at the Budget to give breathing space to businesses because it will mean that more than 70,000 small retail, hospitality and leisure properties are taken out of paying business rates altogether, that pubs will have a 20% cut in their business rates from next April and that business rates for retail, hospitality and leisure premises of all sizes will either fall or be frozen in real terms. In addition to business rates, many firms will benefit from our freeze on red diesel duty and from the reduction in energy bills by up to 25% for more than 10,000 eligible businesses from next April through the British industrial competitiveness scheme. That is what breathing space for businesses looks like, alongside the breathing space for families. As I said earlier, the bedrock of our approach—our lodestar—to the public finances is fiscal discipline. That is why the Budget set out how we will fully fund all new policy and breathing space measures for families and businesses. In deciding his approach, the Chancellor rejected broad-based tax rises, instead taking decisions about tax changes that are fair, proportionate and targeted. That included having banks help pay for the energy help for households this winter through a temporary increase to the bank surcharge and an increase in machine games duty for higher-stakes machines to help fund cuts for business rates.

Could the Minister confirm that, under the current regulatory regime, the £1.5 billion that will be taken over 15 months in this doubled bank tax could be lent out to a maximum of £25 billion? There is a risk that having withdrawn £1.5 billion from the banks’ equity, £25 billion—it is the maximum—in lending to the UK businesses we are talking about could be lost?

I am sure the right hon. Gentleman will have been interested in our measures in the Budget for the British Business Bank, for instance, to increase access to finance, particularly for many of those businesses that are trying to scale up and increase. But I come back to this central point—I know what his position will be because he is a loyal member of the Opposition Benches and will follow what the Leader of the Opposition said on Budget day itself—which is that the Conservative party does not support our decision to require banks to pay a little more for a temporary period of time to fund household support across the country. We know that banks are coming from a strong position. It is a temporary increase. It is one that we believe is fair, targeted and proportionate. We are asking banks—requiring banks—to pay that extra amount, and they are therefore contributing towards the important support for households. What I think is sad about this debate is that the Opposition do not support that breathing space for households. I thought the right hon. Gentleman was loyal to his party leader, but if he would like to break ranks and intervene on me again to confirm that he supports our £100 household energy payment, that would be helpful.

The slavish loyalty of the Minister has already been remarked upon, along with the courage that goes with defending the indefensible quite as often as he has done—always with wit and good humour. Could he address this particular point? The truth is that banks are a popular target to hit with the public and with Labour Members, but if there is actually less money to go to the pubs, restaurants and small businesses in my constituency and elsewhere, can he not accept that that multiple should give people pause for thought before they go for the easy, popular target and take it out of the big, fat, rich banks, if it turns out the small business in trouble will actually lose the credit it desperately needs?

I was listening carefully to the right hon. Gentleman, as I always do whenever he speaks in this Chamber, and I did not hear a response to the question I asked of him, which is whether he supports the household energy payment, which the Leader of the Opposition so clearly opposes. I invited him to intervene to clarify his position given there seems to be some confusion on the Opposition Benches around the household energy payment and whether they support it or not. I would have thought that given the Leader of the Opposition was so clear in not supporting the household energy payment, the hon. Gentleman—

I would have thought that the right hon. Gentleman—excuse me—would have no difficulty in rowing in behind her, but he seems to be struggling with that somewhat, so I will make some progress. I was speaking about the fiscal discipline that underwrites everything we are doing as a Government. Through the approach that we took in the Budget, we have maintained our fiscal rules while making no changes to rates of income tax or national insurance on income from employment or self-employment, or to the rate of national insurance that employers pay on wages or salaries for their staff.

The Minister is giving us lots of opportunity to intervene on him, and we are grateful for that. We keep hearing about the “difficult decisions” that Ministers are making to increase taxes. I do not think that is a difficult decision; it is a very easy decision to make—the laziest decision for a Government. I noticed that his list did not include the new tax on tourism. Will he please explain how Labour believes that we can help an industry by taxing it more?

As the hon. Gentleman may know, the overnight visitor levy is a power that we are giving to strategic authorities across the country. It will be a decision for mayors or foundational strategic authorities to take about whether to introduce that levy, and if they do so, at what percentage to introduce it. Any proceeds will be reinvested in the local visitor economy and other infrastructure in the local area, and will support that area to get more visitors in future, thereby supporting economic growth—I hope that is something the hon. Gentleman would support. Let me turn directly to the role of employers in our country, given the title of the motion. As I said in response to an earlier intervention, employers are working people and they are the backbone of our economy. As I also said, that is why the Budget gives businesses breathing space, with 70,000 retail, hospitality and leisure properties taken out of business rates altogether, and bills for others cut or frozen in real terms.

I thank the right hon. Member for giving way yet again. He is helpfully listing things from the Budget that are supposed to help businesses, but I wonder whether he has come across anyone in his constituency, or in his work at the Treasury who, like businesses I am aware of, have seen the standing charge for their business electricity double. We are talking four figures in the first place, so that is a significant increase. In one case a business invested in solar panels, which the Government would no doubt welcome, but ultimately the investment that it made will be completely wiped out by increased standing charges. Will the Minister address that specific point?

I thank the hon. Lady for mentioning energy bills, because as MPs and Ministers we all recognise that energy costs are one of the primary concerns for households and businesses across the country. In the Budget two weeks ago, we offered breathing space for families and businesses, including with energy bills. Crucially, we also set out the work we will be doing in the years ahead to get those energy bills down for good, and ensure that we can invest in home-grown, renewable cleaner sources of energy, break the link between electricity and gas prices, and remove standing charges from gas bills and then electricity bills. All that is about reforming the way the energy market works, because while breathing space is what households and businesses need now, we know that longer-term reform is needed over time. I was explaining the breathing space for businesses, and I mentioned the cuts to business rates announced in the Budget. I remind hon. Members that we are backing people who want to start and grow businesses by cutting red tape and unlocking billions of pounds of investment. We also introduced our new founders’ relief for founders of high-growth companies, and a new young entrepreneurs allowance to cover a year of living costs for young founders while they bring ideas alive. Employers and businesses drive growth, offer job opportunities and create wealth across our country.

I am sure the Minister will agree that the Conservatives left the high street on life support, but unfortunately I feel that Labour has failed to resuscitate it. Epsom and Ewell has a coffee shop called Brew Forty Two. The staff work really hard, but rising costs mean it is difficult to employ young people, and the Saturday job is pretty much now extinct. Does the Minister agree that we need to reinstate lower national insurance contributions?

I will come to that later in my remarks. Employers do not pay national insurance contributions for under-21s, because of the relief that already exists, or for apprentices under the age of 25. That goes some way towards supporting the objective that the hon. Lady mentions, which is to ensure that employers are supporting young people into work. I agree with her comments about the state in which the Conservatives left high streets across the country, having not done what was necessary to support them over 14 years. Businesses across the country are the ones who drive economic growth, and every employer across the country knows the importance of fiscal discipline. It is crucial in enabling them to succeed, just as it is the crucial bedrock of economic stability for the country and the foundation that we need to support confidence and long-term growth.
I will give way one more time, then I will make a bit of progress.

The Minister is being immensely generous in taking interventions. Employers in my constituency include many farmers and growers and related food firms and hauliers, yet much of the land in my constituency is threatened with immense solar developments, which will take that land out of production. That threatens the country’s food security, and we risk making energy security the enemy of food security. That is bound to undermine our economy in the long term, as we import more and more of what we need to feed the nation. Will he take a look at that, discuss it with colleagues across Government and see how we can reverse that trend? It puts our national economic resilience at risk.

While I agree with the right hon. Gentleman drawing attention to the importance of food security as part of our national security, he and I take a different approach to energy security. The reforms that we are implementing as a Government, including through investment in home-grown, independent sources of energy to increase our energy security and make us more independent from fossil fuel prices around the world, are crucial to bringing bills down over time and ensuring greater energy independence and energy security. That is what the Government are doing, and that is how we see ourselves responding to one of the greatest pressures that many households and businesses face: the immediate and long-term costs of energy. I was talking about employers recognising the importance of fiscal discipline in their own businesses, just as the Government recognise the importance of fiscal discipline for the country. We know that this Government inherited a crisis in our public services, our public finances and the cost of living. NHS waiting lists were at record levels, children worked in portacabins as school roofs crumbled, and rivers were filled with polluted waste. Billions of pounds of spending commitments had not been funded or even properly disclosed to the Office for Budget Responsibility. Faced with that reality, any responsible Government would have to act. We kept our manifesto commitment to working people not to increase their income tax, their national insurance or VAT, and we went further by freezing fuel duty and raising the national minimum wage.

I will make some progress, as I have taken a few interventions. Maybe I will address the hon. Gentleman’s point in a moment. After taking office, we had to take decisions on tax, welfare and spending to fix the public finances and repair our broken public services. It was to restore stability in the public finances and to get our NHS and other essential services back on their feet that we increased national insurance contributions from employers. In making that change, we also more than doubled the employment allowance from £5,000 to £10,500 so that around 900,000 employers—around 40% of employers—have no employer national insurance liability at all. As I mentioned earlier in response to the hon. Member for Epsom and Ewell (Helen Maguire), we maintained reliefs for those employing younger workers, with businesses able to claim employer national insurance contribution reliefs, including for those aged under 21 and apprentices under the age of 25. That means that employers pay no employer national insurance contributions for employees under the age of 21 or apprentices under the age of 25 on earnings up to £50,270, which saves up to £6,750 a year for each eligible employee. We know that the decision to increase employer national insurance contributions had an impact on businesses, but we recognise that because of that choice and others, we have been able to put the NHS back on its feet, with waiting lists down by more than 250,000 since the Government came into power. As well as getting the NHS back on its feet, our fiscal rules and the discipline of meeting them mean that we are boosting investment in Britain’s future—the investment that families and businesses want and need. Across this Parliament, we will invest an additional £120 billion in Britain’s roads, rail, energy and other infrastructure, which is so important for driving growth, and last year we delivered the highest number of affordable homes in a decade.

Does my right hon. Friend agree that this Government’s investment in our infrastructure and our NHS, which is significantly higher than the risible amount of investment delivered under the previous Government, is pro-business and pro-economic growth, and that that is why the Budget measures will help our country and help businesses across this land?

My hon. Friend is absolutely right that businesses want to make sure that the population—their employees or future employees—are healthy, are able to get to work and are able to access the support they need to get a job. That is as important for businesses as it is for the people themselves, and of course businesses want to see the investment in infrastructure that our adherence to our fiscal rules enables. That investment in rail, road and energy is so important to businesses, as it is to families across the country. In their motion, the Conservatives propose halving employer national insurance contributions for under-25s. Apart from a brief mention in the shadow Secretary of State’s speech, they appear to have forgotten that employers already pay no employer national insurance on any earnings up to £50,270 for every employee under 21, and for all apprentices under 25. However, the bigger problem—one that goes to the very heart of why the Conservatives failed in government and why it is clear that they have learned nothing—is that they are very good at announcing tax cuts, yet always entirely fail to credibly say how they would pay for them. If they want a reduction in employer national insurance, what is the cost? Where does the money come from? Is it from higher borrowing, higher taxes on someone else or cuts to the NHS and other public services that working people rely on? Just look at the Conservatives’ announcements on tax more widely. They have promised billions of pounds-worth of unfunded and poorly targeted tax cuts for the very wealthiest—exactly the same irresponsibility that led to the disastrous Liz Truss mini-Budget that crashed the economy and sent mortgages skyrocketing. That is the difference between us as a responsible Government and them as a discredited Opposition.

There is a constant tension in that those who criticise Government fiscal policy must say where they would get the money from. On that basis, could the Minister advise the House what progress the Government have made over the past two years on closing the tax gap, and say what size it currently is?

If the hon. Gentleman wants to have a conversation about the tax gap, I am very happy to pick that up. When we came into office in 2024, one of our first priorities was to close the tax gap before asking for any further tax contributions from any other sources. That was an essential part of our wider plan to restore public services and the public finances and to create the conditions for economic growth.
