That work continues, and I am very pleased to be playing a role in the Treasury, continuing that work to close the tax gap and modernise the service His Majesty’s Revenue and Customs provides, so that more people pay the right tax first time and can pay it automatically without mistakes or errors creeping into the system. Because of the decisions we have taken as a Government—including closing the tax gap, as the hon. Member for Angus and Perthshire Glens (Dave Doogan) mentioned— we are providing certainty and stability. Meanwhile, the Conservative party cannot resist playing games with the public finances, irrespective of the fact that whenever it has done so in the past, it is working people who have suffered the most. Britain is a country of entrepreneurs, shopkeepers, manufacturers, publicans, start-ups, family firms and growing businesses, and I am proud of the people across our country who take on risk and put in every hour they can to start and grow businesses. Above all, they need—and they have—a Government who are prepared to do the hard work of building a stable economy in which businesses can prosper. Employers need stability in order to plan for the future, create good jobs, invest and innovate, and providing that foundation is our responsibility as a Government. That is why, in the face of global storms, fiscal discipline will always underwrite every promise this Government make. The opposite is true of the Conservative party. Government is about making choices, not pretending that choices do not exist. We in this Government are choosing to back working people. We are choosing to back the employers who create jobs. We are choosing to back young people into work, and we will always choose, with fiscal discipline as our lodestar, to maintain the economic stability on which our success as a country depends. For all those reasons, I urge Members to reject the motion.

It has been a tough decade for businesses. It all started with Brexit, which unleashed uncertainty, red tape and form-filling, pushing up prices for all of us. Following that was the covid pandemic. Notwithstanding the furlough scheme, it unleashed on business a boom and bust cycle of lockdowns and opening back up, all because the then Conservative Government did not buy an off-the-shelf app that might have prevented that boom and bust cycle by tracking the impact.
I recall that when I was sat on the Government Benches, the Liberal Democrats were calling for more stringent measures.

The right hon. Gentleman will perhaps remember more correctly that during that time we called for a lockdown initially, but the public had already decided to go into lockdown. He will also remember that the then Prime Minister announced that pubs, high streets and a whole load of businesses should be closing down, without covering their insurance. The right hon. Gentleman will remember that. Following covid, we had the mini-Budget, which I am sure the Conservatives will deny, too. The mini-Budget was incredibly painful and unleashed huge panic in the financial markets. It drove up the cost of living and the cost of commercial loans. On top of all that, we then had two anti-growth Budgets from the Labour Government that have pushed up costs on businesses. For many, it is too much to bear. Small businesses, the backbone of our high streets and our communities, have borne the brunt. It is the cumulative impact that small businesses have expressed concern about. They tell me that if it had been just one tax, they might just have been able to manage it, but they have had the national insurance contributions rise, the business rates changes and the Employment Rights Act 2025, which got the balance wrong between protections for workers and the burden on business. Businesses that have put in blood, sweat and tears and financial investment are now struggling and do not know whether they can survive.

The hon. Lady has given a comprehensive list of the impediments that this Government have put the way of business in just 24 months, but I hope she will not forget that we have the highest commercial energy prices anywhere in the developed world under this Labour Government. Those are similarly threatening to put businesses under.

The hon. Gentleman is right to raise the fact that we have some of the highest energy costs for business. We have called on the Government to extend their scheme for energy-intensive businesses. We have made it clear that we want to see further action on decoupling the link between gas and electricity. I have had meetings with Ofgem about making sure that there is better regulation for small businesses, particularly when they are looking to brokers for their energy deals. There needs to be far more action, not just for energy-intensive businesses, but for the small businesses on our high streets. As I was saying, the impact on businesses of all these higher taxes has exacerbated the youth unemployment problem. That is why we now see vacancies at a five-year low. It is wrong to blame young people for not applying for or getting jobs when there simply are not jobs for them to apply for. That is why we Liberal Democrats have talked about growing our economy and pulling the biggest single growth lever that we can by joining the single market, which would reduce costs for businesses.

Have the Liberal Democrats done any modelling of what the impact would be on those young people who are not employed if we rejoined the European Union and had free movement or if we had a youth mobility approach and there was an influx of young people into this country?

If there are no jobs in the UK, there will not be people coming to the UK to take jobs that do not exist. If we could join the single market, it would reduce red tape, reduce form-filling, and make it cheaper for businesses in the UK to grow. They would create more jobs, and there would be more jobs for young people. I simply cannot believe that the Conservative party, despite all the evidence and all the studies, will still not accept that having a stronger relationship with Europe is the single biggest way in which we can grow our economy—and it is only if we grow our economy that we can cut taxes and cut bills. For as long as the Conservatives refuse to acknowledge the damage of their Brexit deal, they will remain an out-of-touch, anti-growth, anti-business party.

The hon. Lady has made the argument here eloquently, many times, about joining the single market and the customs union. However, on 1 April 2019, the House came within three votes of a Brexit deal that would have allowed the retention of membership of the customs union. I voted for it, and others who were Labour Members at the time voted for it. Six Liberal Democrats, including the current leader of the hon. Lady’s party, voted against it. They walked into the Lobby with the Conservatives—with those of the right—to veto a Brexit deal that included membership of the customs union. Why did they do that?
I will not apologise for the fact that we fought tooth and nail—we were the only large party that fought tooth and nail—to stop the damage of the Brexit deal in any shape or form.

In the last Parliament, the SNP was a substantially bigger party than the Liberal Democrats, and we fought tooth and nail to maintain membership of the EU as well. I am sure the hon. Lady will acknowledge that.

I do indeed acknowledge that. It was a slip of the tongue. Many parties were fighting tooth and nail to stop the damage of the Conservatives’ botched Brexit deal. I hope very much that at the EU summit, the Labour Government will move a great deal further than the timid approach they appear to be taking now.

Will the hon. Lady acknowledge that economic growth in Europe is lower than the economic growth in this country? Perhaps she could also tell the House how much her party, under its policy proposal, would be willing to pay to join the single market. Would that not take money out of the economy that we could be using to increase growth domestically?

The hon. Gentleman will, I hope, accept that growth in one country is not equivalent to growth in another country. When we tear down barriers between countries, we increase growth. Plenty of modelling has been done by the national economic social research unit in America, and by other bodies in this country. I am not sure, but I believe it is PwC that has talked about the amount of growth we would gain from the single market. We believe that joining the single market and the customs union would bring in about £29 billion and that the cost would probably be about £2 billion, so the growth that we would gain would massively exceed the cost of joining.
Does the hon. Lady agree that the Liberal Democrats are a singularly special party in this place, because they can believe passionately in something and then not vote for it?

I am sure that if I had more time to speak in this debate, I could point to a number of examples of the Conservative party saying one thing and doing another. It is, of course, a party that is trying to claim, after the mini-Budget, that it is reclaiming the brand of fiscal responsibility, but even in the Conservatives’ recent spending plans there is, according to my calculation, a £33 billion hole between their funding pledges—or the things they want to fund—and the tax cuts that they want to make. It looks like Trussonomics 2.0.

May I bring the hon. Lady back to the point about the opportunity presented by opening up greater access to the European single market? She has cited various reports suggesting that that would be good. Is she aware of the winners of the Nobel prize for economics last year, who demonstrated that what has driven growth across the world, but particularly in the United Kingdom, has not been access to wider markets, but innovation and technology? That is about the growth that we receive from supporting businesses to develop new products and services. It is not access to global markets that does that; it is our own industry and services economy here in the UK. Will the hon. Lady please return to the original liberal principles that helped to develop the prosperity of this country in the 19th and 20th centuries, which are about low tax and low regulation?

I have made it very clear in my speech that the single biggest lever for growth is a much better deal with Europe. I have never said that it is the only lever for growth. I absolutely believe that we need to invest in innovation, and I wish that the Government would go further in fixing the entire pipeline, from ideas and start-ups to scale-ups and commercialisation. We should be the best place in the world for a business to start up, to scale up and to stay, and I hope that the hon. Gentleman shares that vision. I return to the motion. I was saying that the rise in national insurance contributions has exacerbated youth unemployment. We want growth with Europe; we want NICs cut; we want 100 hours of guaranteed work experience for young people before they reach the age of 18; and we want the cliff edges in universal credit tackled as well. We are pleased that the Labour Government have finally looked at putting a tax on the banks, but they will be aware that we have pointed out other ways in which they could have raised taxes on the banks—for example, through a windfall tax on unearned income, which would not deter any further investment. When it comes to our economy and supporting employers, the only long-term solution is to get growth back into our country and get Britain growing again. That is the only way that we can cut taxes and bills.
Order. To ensure that everybody can contribute, there will be a speaking limit of seven minutes for Back Benchers.

I want to start a bit differently today, if I may. My parents were employers; they were business people. They employed me in what was probably my first job. As the son of immigrants, I did not get a choice as to whether I took up that employment. I am not quite sure if I was paid the minimum wage, but working taught me something. It taught me what it meant to earn money; it taught me the pride in work; and it taught me what I got at the end of it. I will never forget working for a week, and then buying a turquoise iPod Mini. I loved that iPod, partly because I was really hip and cool, of course—

Stop it! The hon. Member is too kind. I had a sense of pride, because I knew that I had earned that iPod; it was the fruits of my labour. When I was growing up in the ’90s and ’00s, I saw business people doing well, partly because we were growing under a Labour Government, but also because the conditions of business worked. My parents knew that their workers had skills and were healthy, and they also knew that workers and families across the country were living good lives at that point in time. They could afford a decent life, and to spend money down the shops and on the goods that my parents were producing and selling. I saw them do well, and I saw business do well. Part of the reason why I became a member of the Labour party is that I want to see every single person do well and thrive. I saw businesses thrive, and I saw my parents’ business thrive. I also joined the Labour party because we are the party of work—the clue is in the name. I want every single person in this country to have a good job, but we are quite far away from that, and we have been for quite a while. About 40% of people in full-time work cannot afford to raise a family, because there are not enough good jobs in this country. Post-industrial areas are still post-industrial, and they are the most deprived parts of this nation. They have not been doing well for an incredibly long time. We have to do more to create good jobs across our country.
I could not agree more. We should do everything to create jobs. Surely the hon. Member is about to suggest that we cut taxes on businesses. That will create jobs.

I want to start there. I disagree with the Conservatives’ motion. It effectively says that if we cut national insurance contributions, good jobs will follow. The first thing to note is that, yes, we did raise national insurance contributions in our first Budget, and there are a million more people in work today. The second thing to note is that the Conservatives’ mistaken moral aims would lead to poorer material ends. They are googling; they are finding out the difference between the pay-as-you-earn measure of employment and the Office for National Statistics measure of employment. There is something else on which I disagree with the Conservatives. I read the document entitled “The Right Way”, which they produced before their conference. It effectively said that if the Government just step away and create the right conditions, businesses will create the prosperity and good jobs that we need. We have seen that this has not worked. Post-industrial areas are still post-industrial. We saw the Government step away in the 1980s, and we saw those areas remain poor over time. In places like Middlesbrough, the employment rate is 20 percentage points lower than the national average. For non-graduate men, the employment rate is down by about 20 percentage points, too.

The hon. Member is talking about deindustrialisation; it is happening right now in my constituency, because we are turning our back on the oil and gas industry. We are not approving Rosebank, when we should. It is an absolute disgrace that the Labour Government are killing off jobs right across north-east Scotland.

I think about 90% of jobs in the oil and gas industry have disappeared over the past 20 or 30 years, including 150,000 in Aberdeen. That is basically because the North sea is a declining basin; we cannot change geological facts. As the hon. Member will know, the Rosebank decision is a quasi-judicial one that will be made by the Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero. I come back to the fact that in the 1980s, the Conservatives said, “If you just cut taxes, good times will follow,” but they did not follow for huge numbers of people and huge areas of this country. We also see the legacy of the Conservative Governments from 2010 to 2024: in the past few years, there have been 250,000 more young people not in education, employment or training; areas have not recovered; and there has been the longest wage stagnation since Napoleon’s time. We have seen the outcomes of the Conservatives’ philosophy. They had 14 years in government, and it was not a success. We did not see good jobs across this nation, because there was not the means or materials for them, or a foundation of prosperity. There were not the skills; the number of apprenticeship starts for young people was down by a third. The population was not healthy; we had the longest waiting lists on record. There was not enough transport infrastructure—ours was the worst in western Europe—and energy costs were the highest in the G7. That was the legacy of your Government, because the only thing Conservative Members have ever believed—
Order. I am not participating in this debate, but presiding over it, so “you” and “your” are not needed.
I will give way, because the right hon. Member has been very patient.

. The hon. Member is being most generous in giving way. He is a fair-minded man, so, on outcomes, I am slightly surprised that he picks this figure of 1 million more people in work; the numbers from His Majesty’s Revenue and Customs show that the payroll has reduced by 165,000 people since July 2024, and that the number of unemployed people has gone up by 225,000. In fairness, would he make sure that he does not just pick the one statistic that he thinks helps his argument?

I choose to use the labour force survey statistic because it includes both the self-employed and those who are low-paid and do not appear in the PAYE figures. I pick that figure because it is more comprehensive, and I believe it is more correct, as it includes everybody in work. I want to briefly pick up the point about unemployment. The right hon. Member is right to say that both employment and unemployment have increased, but that in part is good news; it is because those who were economically inactive are now seeking work, so they are now in the category of “unemployed”, rather than “inactive”. We have more people in work, and more people looking for work. Our argument is that, for businesses to create prosperity, they need not just lower taxes—I take the Opposition’s point on that—but the sales and the foundations to create prosperity. They need a healthy workforce. That is why we are investing in the NHS and waiting lists are falling. They need good skills, which is why the number of apprenticeship starts in this country is such a focus for this Government. They also need lower energy costs, which means providing home-grown, cheaper, cleaner energy. Those things help employers produce more in this country, and help businesses hire more people.

I am very grateful to my Leicestershire colleague for giving way. Could he point to where in the Budget Loughborough cafés or restaurants will get specific support with their energy? The British industrial competitiveness scheme is only for manufacturing, and all the tax levies that are coming off bills—the carbon taxes, the green levies—will not do so until 2028. I am not aware of any support specifically for cafés in Loughborough or restaurants on his high street. Am I wrong?

As the hon. Member will know, we are also freezing rates, but on a personal note, I do everything I can to support every pub in my constituency, because that is the service we Labour Members believe in. We know that our approach, our philosophy and our moral aim leads to material prosperity because we have seen it before. We saw Attlee create collective prosperity after collective sacrifice, and Blair and Brown renew a nation after 18 years of Conservative Government. We see how our aims lead to better outcomes. Labour Members believe that our country thrives when everybody thrives. Businesses do well when everybody does well—when the young person who leaves school knows that they can get a good job in a local business; when that business can hire them, because it knows that they have the skills that it needs; and, more importantly, when the business knows that consumers can buy its goods, because we are making life affordable for all. That is how we Labour Members are creating jobs and helping business people like my mum and dad.

It is a pleasure to speak in this debate, and to listen to a range of views, but I genuinely think that Government Members should begin with an apology to employers, for a number of reasons. First of all, the Chief Secretary to the Treasury insulted them all a few weekends ago, basically saying that employers are not working people. It was a flat insult to the millions upon millions of people in family-run businesses, probably just like the parents of the hon. Member for Loughborough (Dr Sandher), who just gave a lecture on his views about employment and employability. Fundamentally, small and medium-sized enterprises—hard-working family-run businesses—have always been the backbone of Britain and the British economy. I have a lot of time for the Minister. He is a great survivor, and he deserves some kind of accolade for his long-standing defence of his Government’s tax-grabbing, job-destroying policies, and even for his references to fiscal discipline—we can talk about that—but the Government need to wake up to the adverse impact of their economic policies for employment. We see devastating impacts on small businesses across the country and their ability to function. They are working hard and putting in long hours just to keep the lights on and manage their cash flow. The Government need to demonstrate some humility and acknowledge that right now.

I thank my right hon. Friend for her assessment of the performance of the Government Front Benchers—I tried to intervene on the Minister. I have serious concerns; the Minister said, at the Dispatch Box, “We kept our manifesto commitment not to tax working people.” He then said that they introduced a NICs increase for employers, but in the same breath, he said, “Employers are working people.” Do you not agree with me that the Minister clearly does not understand what a business is, and that, in increasing NICs, he has increased taxes on working people and broken a manifesto promise?
Order. Once again, “you” and “your” are not to be used when referencing colleagues.

My hon. Friend is absolutely right. I do not want to insult anybody, but it is important for Members to speak on these issues if they have credible experience of them—if they have set up a business and come from a business background. I am afraid that government has become a blunt instrument now. Things are far too binary. The Government are not even thinking through the overall impact of their decisions on local businesses, and then they come to the Dispatch Box defending broken pledges. This House should spend much more time talking about our pride in the nation’s businesses. They are the wealth creators and employers who give people a hand up in life. They give people economic security. I will speak for my great county of Essex, because I do not think it gets enough airtime in this Chamber. We are a county of entrepreneurs. Despite the damage that this job-destroying, business-bashing, tax-grabbing Labour Government are doing to our economy, we are fighting hard to survive. We have a range of amazing businesses, and I will list them, because I think the House might have experienced some of the fine produce from Essex. Wilkin and Sons in Tiptree makes the jam that is in the Tea Room. Linden Lady chocolates, made in Copford, are sold in the House of Commons shop. There is a range of Essex farmers and food manufacturers, whom we all depend on. A colleague spoke about food security; that matters. Maldon Salt, a very famous brand, comes from my constituency as well. On the Opposition Front Bench, my hon. Friend the Member for Hornchurch and Upminster (Julia Lopez) touched on pubs, salons and all those other employers that provide the gateway to jobs for young people. Those are the types of business that we must support—we absolutely need to give them a hand up right now. We need reductions in national insurance, and we must recognise that in a significant way. Businesses think that Labour Ministers have no idea about the fact that they are working 70 or 80 hours a week just to keep their businesses afloat. That work is to generate tax revenues that this wasteful and bloated socialist Government are, quite frankly, destroying in an unjustifiable way. There must be a recognition, because businesses in my constituency feel let down by Labour and seriously want to fight back against the increase in national insurance, the red tape from the infamous Employment Rights Act 2026 and the taxes on family farms. Businesses are constantly facing a rising tax burden. Even the reliefs in the recent Budget, which Ministers want to gloat about, will not compensate for the overall pain that businesses are facing. The Minister spoke about fiscal discipline, but fiscal discipline alongside high levels of borrowing and debt will not give the financial and economic stability that local businesses need in our country. Debt is not going down, and borrowing is going up. We know who pays for all that: businesses pay for it all. Ministers come and go—we all know that—and they can make whatever defence they wish, but the reality is that it is hard-pressed taxpayers who are constantly filling Government coffers right now for higher debt and borrowing. Businesses need some latitude and leeway—they really do. I implore and urge this Government to reconsider many of the policies that they are putting in place. There is a silver lining; it is called the Finance Bill. When that sees the light of day on the Floor of this House, it will give Members the opportunity to challenge the Government to give headroom and breathing space to businesses by lowering taxes, being more responsible on national insurance contributions and freeing up businesses to employ more people. Importantly, it will give Members the opportunity to challenge the Government to give the British people the freedom to succeed and live their lives, completely unshackled from the burdensome taxes that this Government are constantly putting on them.

Like the right hon. Member for Witham (Priti Patel), I start by recognising the many amazing employers and businesses across my constituency, from large household names such as Aviva, to local SMEs, including MSI Defence Systems, and local retail and hospitality businesses that are the backbones of our high streets, such as Café 193. I recognise the pressures on employers and businesses, including in the face of external shocks. I will focus on relaying some of the messages that I have heard from businesses and employers in my constituency. I welcome the targeted measures in last month’s Budget, as the Minister set out, including the business rates relief. That will mean that more than half of all retail, hospitality and leisure businesses in the east of England will pay no rates at all, and another 900 businesses in Norwich and 400 in Broadland will benefit from frozen rates. I recently attended a roundtable hosted by the New Anglia Advanced Manufacturing and Engineering partnership. Many of those innovative businesses are creating products and jobs in Britain—including for my constituents in Norfolk—but they face challenges. One of the biggest challenges they raised, which will not surprise the Minister, was rising high industrial energy costs, which are affecting trade and regional growth. I welcome the action that the Government are taking with BICS, but I urge the Minister to set out what more we can do to support manufacturing businesses such as those at the roundtable. Today, we have had good news in the press that £12 billion of investment has been secured to build the Vanguard East and West wind farms off the coast of Norfolk. Those schemes alone will create more than 2,400 jobs, and I want as many of them as possible to be for people from Norfolk. We have to ensure that employers can also benefit from the supply chains. Norfolk has many strengths; renewable energy is just one of them. We have a £20 billion economy and strengths in energy, agrifood, advanced manufacturing, financial services and world-class research, such as at the Norwich research park. When the new Prime Minister came into office, the Norfolk and Suffolk business boards wrote to him together to set out how Norfolk and Suffolk can help to power, feed, connect and innovate the UK’s future. That is the ambition that I have heard from businesses. I have also heard businesses’ requests that the Government work with them in three key ways that will benefit employers in Norfolk and Suffolk. First, as we have touched on already in this debate, is the importance of backing nationally significant infrastructure projects such as the Bacton energy hub and the desperately needed upgrade at Ely and Haughley junctions. Despite our differences across the House, I know that MPs across East Anglia really support those investments because of the impact they will have on businesses in the area. Secondly, through innovation we could be the leading testbed for new technologies, building on world-class assets such as the Norwich research park. Thirdly, by aligning skills, innovation and industrial policy, we will help businesses to invest, create jobs and develop the workforces they need. Another clear message I have heard—we have touched on the need for stability—is about devolution and the opportunity it presents for employers and businesses. I welcome Norfolk and Suffolk being on track for devolution. This week, the Reform-led Norfolk and Suffolk county councils have finally reached an agreement on the terms of a devolution deal, which the Government are backing with about £37 million of investment each year. That cannot come soon enough; we need that deal and the associated funding in place as quickly as possible so that we can invest in infrastructure, skills and economic growth. It is really important that employers and businesses’ voices are heard and that they are instrumental in seeing how that investment is spent. I will not pretend that I have not heard message

It is a pleasure to contribute to this debate and to follow the hon. Member for Norwich North (Alice Macdonald). I heard a collective thud when the Minister was speaking earlier, which must have been the jaws of businesses in my constituency hitting the floor, because there was a real lack of understanding of the real pressures that businesses are facing. One thing I love about being a Member of Parliament is spending time going around the constituency, and I always make a point of visiting businesses—be they small, medium or large—to hear directly from them their concerns, and there are many of them. I also hold a regular business club, and it is becoming increasingly difficult in those meetings to give businesses any meaningful answers of reassurance because of the real problems they are facing. I am always struck by just how hard these people are working to keep their businesses going. They are part of not just our local economy, but our community. They create the vibrancy of our villages and our towns and are places where people can meet and congregate. These things are really important. We heard a moment ago about tech and innovation; even in the smallest barn on a farm, some really amazing tech companies are being created, and that is something we should be celebrating. Employers want their businesses to be successful, and having a great team of employees is a keen part of that. Employers invest not only financially but emotionally in their business. I hear time and again that the costs of running a business are making that increasingly difficult. The spokesperson for the Liberal Democrats, the hon. Member for St Albans (Daisy Cooper), was right to say that a multitude of tax rises are creating that difficulty—not least the Government’s increase in employer national insurance contributions. The Government will point to the increase in employer allowance, and I appreciate that it helps some businesses, but it does not change the fundamental fact that many employers are facing higher costs just to employ the same people and local businesses are having to make really difficult decisions. Time and again I hear it. I was depressed to hear at one event about a business whose owner had started it three years ago on his own and that was about to employ three people, but the national insurance contribution rise meant that that simply was not affordable any more. It is not just businesses that are affected. Time and again, when I was a shadow Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Minister, I tried to raise the impact on the charities sector, where I spent 16 years working before entering Parliament. I know the pressures that they face. I particularly worked in hospices, which can only provide care if they can afford to employ the people to look after their residents—children, in the case of the hospice I worked in. The Government will cite their £100 million of capital funding for hospices, but they cannot fund nurses with bricks and mortar. The reality is that these workers should not be facing these tax rises, because they are picking up a massive part of public sector work in caring for some of the most vulnerable people in our constituencies. We have many wonderful charities in my constituency that provide important services to people who need them. They are employers too, and they still have staff to pay. When I speak to the people who use these charity services, it is not the charity that they talk about but the staff. That is why we must think about those charities as well.

In my constituency of Newbury, a volunteer centre survey found that charities needed to raise an additional £300,000 a year just to stand still. Does the right hon. Member agree that charities’ time should be focused on serving our constituents rather than worrying about fundraising off the back of Labour’s tax rises?

The hon. Gentleman is right. I was the head of fundraising at the hospice, so I know that it takes some time to plan a fundraising strategy. If a charity suddenly finds overnight that it has to find all that extra money, it will be almost impossible, and often they will end up having to eat into reserves, which is not a good thing.

I want to go back to the point that I raised to the shadow Secretary of State. The right hon. Gentleman was here when the health and social care levy came around. At no point did the Conservatives attempt to exempt charities and hospices from that tax rise. Why was it appropriate to keep them in scope when he was proposing it but completely inappropriate now?

I point the hon. Gentleman to his party’s own manifesto. Labour promised that it would not do it. That is the reality of it, and that is the challenge that we are putting to this Government. I really am worried about the opportunities for so many young people. We all remember how important getting our first job was. Mine was being a waiter at a hotel in Anglesey. It taught me about independence, it built my confidence, and it gave me real experience of working, sometimes with very challenging customers. It was really important to build that confidence. But it is becoming increasingly difficult for young people. I know that employers in my constituency want to give young people those opportunities, but there is a cost involved in taking on and training someone. I spoke to one of the pub owners in my constituency who said that he always used to employ 14-year-olds to wash dishes, and when they got a bit older they would work as a waiter or waitress in the restaurant, and when they were a bit older still they would work behind the bar. As a result, he had trained staff, when they came back from university at Christmas or summer. He simply cannot afford to do that any more because of all the additional costs. Instead, he is employing older people. That is a real problem that we have got to address. Many people who have just finished university or further education will be trying to get their first job, often without much experience. We should be doing all we can to encourage employers to give them that chance. That is why I support the Opposition’s proposal to halve employer national insurance contributions for under-25s, which would help businesses to plan ahead when taking on younger employers, making it more affordable to employ those who are just starting out. If we do not address this problem, there is a real danger that young people will find themselves permanently stuck in unemployment. I will make another point to conclude. Some Members talk about employers as though they are somehow separate from working people, but when I visit businesses across my Daventry constituency, I meet people who are working extremely long hours and have often had to put their savings into getting the business up and running in the first place and to keep it afloat. They are serving customers, they are dealing with suppliers and they are doing the accounts. Sometimes they are worrying about whether they will have enough money left to pay themselves, let alone their workforce. They say to me that they wake up in the middle of the night worrying about where the money will come from. I do not think anyone could seriously suggest that those people are not working hard. They are making great personal sacrifices. We should be proud of everything they do and give them encouragement whenever we can. We should welcome the fact that they are providing employment for other people. I want to see businesses in my constituency and across the country doing well, our local charities continuing their important work, and young people having the opportunity to get into employment, but we must recognise that increasing the cost of employing people has consequences, particularly for smaller businesses. Halving employers’ national insurance for under-25s would be a practical way of helping businesses give more young people a chance in life and the start that I enjoyed. For those reasons, I will happily vote for the motion.

I want to speak in the debate because Cornwall probably has more self-employed and small businesses than many other places. Small businesspeople hold businesses together and employ people. They take on the responsibility, risk and privilege of creating jobs for other people. I considered myself as much of a working person when I was an equity partner in a law firm that employed 50 people as I did when I was a teaching assistant. Small businesses do an incredibly important job. I want to talk about a few of them in my constituency. Richard Wakeham at Treveague campsite in Gorran employs six people. We also have Mariners and Harbour Lights, our brilliant fish and chip shops; Bread & Butter in Truro; Fudge & More in St Mawes; and Windjammer, with Oliver running a number of establishments brilliantly. Of course, we have our farmers—I went to see one in Restronguet at the weekend—and then we have publicans like Mark Holden, who runs a number of pubs and has built his hospitality business over 16 years. For many years, Mark has worked hard with young people, setting up apprenticeships and giving training to dozens of Cornish young people. He is working closely with the Government and the Minister for Skills to set up skills training in hospitality down in Cornwall. The motion concentrates on under-25s, so that is what I will focus on. Our young people have struggled, with rising numbers of NEETs, but that has been over a long time, not just the last two years, as the Milburn review made clear. Alan Milburn said that this has been a growing issue, and among the reasons for that are: how SEND provision in schools dropped off under the previous Government; covid, which was a really big issue for young people and hit their confidence; and mental health support, with child and adolescent mental health services having been decimated in the last 15 years. As has been pointed out a number of times, employers pay no national insurance contributions on earnings of up to £50,270 for under-21s, nor for apprentices under 25. That makes a saving of up to £6,790 per employee per year, which was worth £2.5 billion in the last year. Some of the Opposition Members have talked about the minimum wage rises. When the Labour Government first brought in the minimum wage, the figure was similar for everybody over 18, and businesses did not shut down and the economy did not stop, as the Opposition said would happen. When they got into power, they split the minimum wage into three or four different age brackets. That caused an awful lot of problems and inequity, because a 20-year-old’s rent is not cheaper than a 26-year-old’s. In trying to converge those wage differences, we are trying to reintroduce that fairness and the idea of the minimum wage in the first place. This Government have introduced other measures to help small and medium-sized employers take on young people: £2,000 for SMEs that hire apprentices between 16 and 21; free training for under-25 apprentices; the youth jobs grant, with £3,000 for every young person hired; and the jobs guarantee, which is coming in, for fully subsidised jobs for six months, with the Government covering 100% of the employment costs. There are a thousand people in that first pilot. There is a lot of work to be done. Under-25s have struggled for many reasons over a number of years, not just because of the job market. What we have to do, and what the Milburn review will make very clear in the next few weeks that we should do, is support those young people to overcome their barriers and help employers to employ them again.

I rise in support of the Opposition motion. I rise to criticise this Government’s attitude towards employers, their disregard for the reality of life running a business, their nonsensical approach to tackling poverty and social mobility, and their maddening approach to the economy. The reality is that a job is the foundational unit in an economy. It is the immortal gene that is fundamental to economic evolution, growth and prosperity. I say that because a job is, first and foremost, an income. An income keeps a roof over someone’s head, food on the table and the lights on. An income is spent and then passes through the economic supply chain, creating more value and, yes, more jobs. A job is not just an income, however; it is a source of pride, purpose and identity. It offers structure, routine and the opportunity for a sense of self-achievement. It is a source of social inclusion, friendship and support. It is also a stepping stone. The job someone has today connects them to the job opportunity that might come up tomorrow, next week or next month. Without a job today, the probability of being in work in future diminishes greatly. As a result of those three realities, work is indeed the best route out of poverty and into prosperity, not just for the individual but for the population as a whole. Look what happens when work is degraded. All the evidence shows that long-term unemployment is synonymous with depression, anxiety, social isolation and a shortened life expectancy. The Health Foundation found that people out of work and on benefits are five times more likely to report poor health than those in work. And yet, Members on the Labour Benches are obsessed with talking down the importance of a job. They talk of bad jobs and unfulfilling work. The reality is that the phenomenal growth in employment we experienced between 2010 and the onset of covid coincided with a massive improvement in living standards and a fall in material deprivation. If Members do not believe me, they should read the report from the Institute for Fiscal Studies. The share of children living in material deprivation fell by a quarter in the six years leading up to the pandemic. By 2017-18, severe material deprivation among working-age families was roughly one fifth lower than it was in 2010. Pensioner material deprivation fell continuously from 2010 onward. Why? Because rising employment and earned income, offset the cuts to welfare. That is what we delivered in government: a high-employment, low-welfare economy, which is in stark contrast to the high-unemployment and high-welfare economy that this Government aspire to. The Government talk about hope. The Conservatives in government gave people hope of a life off welfare and in work. Four million new jobs were created between 2010 and 2024—4 million people who otherwise would have been left languishing on benefits, 4 million people who could go home on a Friday proud of their contribution to the economy, their family and themselves. The Labour Government cannot help themselves but steam in and ruin the jobs market for so many. Nowhere is that more the case than in their deluded decision to increase national insurance contributions for employers. Can you imagine the contorted logic of saying, “I am from the Labour party, the party of work, and we want jobs for all, so we have decided to tax the people who create the jobs in the hope that taking money out of their pockets will inevitably mean they will have more money to put into yours.” It does not make any sense. This Government do not make any sense. They are for Europe, then they are against it, then they are for it again. They want to invest in defence, then they do not, then they do and now they do not. They embarked on the famous prawn sandwich offensive in advance of the last election, only to turn around and backtrack on all that pro-business sentiment. They promised they would not tax working people, then they did. In the process, we saw a Treasury
Order. I call Danny Kruger, after whose speech the time limit will drop to six minutes.

I want to acknowledge the contributions made by Labour Members, because I think they have clearly articulated their philosophy of growth. In a sense, it is coherent and respectable, because what they believe is that the economic growth is driven by state action. It is true, and they often make this point, that we need the rule of law, infrastructure and proper investment in people, in places and in the sectors that need help. Those are legitimate arguments, but the fact is that our economy is built on businesses. It is built by businesses—particularly small businesses—being free to operate themselves. The prosperity of this country historically was created by free men and women trading with each other with minimal Government regulation. Yes, this took place in a safe and rule-bound world, but with rules that were light and predictable and without excessive taxation. I think of Marlborough, in the heart of my constituency. This wonderful ancient town was given its charter 800 years ago, and it was a successful trading community on the road between London and Bristol. It was built on the textile trade, with amazing wool manufacture and processing. That is what made it rich. I was honoured to join the procession of the town council to the war memorial on Sunday—we love a procession in Marlborough—and to walk behind the robed councillors and mace bearers proclaiming the ancient wealth of the town. The economy of Marlborough now largely involves retail, hospitality and tourism. As the procession walked into St Mary’s church, we passed Franklyn’s Bistro, a restaurant I know well—I was in only a month or two ago—and I saw that, to my great regret, it has now closed altogether. This happens in hospitality. Restaurants open and close, but there is something happening in Marlborough and across my constituency and across the country, which is that hospitality is absolutely on its knees. Worst of all, Marlborough received the terrible news this week that the Polly Tea Rooms had closed down. It was an institution in the town, open for 114 years and surviving two world wars and all the economic ups and downs of the last century and more. This large shop front on the high street had been selling tea and cakes and lunch and dinner for all those decades. I was very proud to be able to support the Polly during covid, and I was very proud that the owner said, “You have saved the Polly,” because I helped him with managing his application for a covid loan, but I am afraid to say that it is all over. I want to quote the notice that the owner, David Clarke, put out: “I have decided to close the Polly Tearooms with immediate effect. I was hoping that the budget…would offer some help to businesses like ours, but the result was the same as every budget this Government has brought in, quite the opposite…Fuel costs and business rates have also been increasing all of the time, but with the cost of living crisis as it is, we simply can’t increase our prices to our customers and expect them to still come in as often as they did in the past. The Chancellor John Healey spoke in his budget…of ‘hope’ for the future. He said the word so many times, I lost count. He sounded like Mr Micawber from David Copperfield, hoping something will turn up. But that is all this government has—hope. No plan for growth, no idea what to do, just hoping something will turn up, rather than creating the environment and conditions to make the economy grow. They are spending far too much money on the wrong things, and then taxing the very people who would be able to create growth to the level that they have nothing left to achieve any of it. The measure for the government investing in anything should be how will this improve our economy. They should apply this test to every penny they spend—literally every penny. But this of course is not what…Labour…do. So, along with literally hundreds of other businesses, I have no option but to give up trying to make it work.” I could not put it

I am really sad to hear about the Polly Tea Rooms in the hon. Gentleman’s constituency, but has he spoken to the IFS about cutting VAT? The IFS has said that cutting VAT would not generate the income that people promise, and I think the Treasury says the same. For businesses like the Polly Tea Rooms, I do understand the issue of the national insurance rise in the Budget of two years ago, but the other issue is the cost of living crisis, which is driven by something we have not spoken about in this debate at all: Trump’s war on Iran. Does he recognise those wider impacts on the economy as well?

I do not accept for a second that cutting VAT on hospitality would not be of great benefit to those businesses. I am astonished to hear that the IFS might have said such a thing. VAT is one of the major costs that businesses have to carry, so clearly a cut in what is essentially a sales tax for retail businesses would be helpful. I will speak briefly about the challenge of the cost of living and energy costs in particular, because the issue for retail businesses like the Polly is not just about the costs that they have to carry; it is about the demand for their business being reduced because of the cost of living that customers are carrying, as Mr Clarke said in the statement I read out. What the Government should do is not simply give people more money to spend, but ensure a stable economy and a stable society, and then leave people with more of their own money that they can spend on our high streets. That is why my party proposes raising the personal allowance for individual taxpayers to £15,000. That would be a tax cut of £500 per person for over 40 million people in this country. On the point made by the hon. Member for Edinburgh South West (Dr Arthur), I say that we would take £250 off household energy bills, which is the right response to the accelerating energy costs that have been caused not just by global instability but by Labour’s obsession with net zero.
Order. There is now a five-minute speaking limit for Back Benchers.

British businessmen and women are integral to the growth and sustainability of our nation’s finances. A nation’s economic strength is measured not simply by the size of its Government, the amount it spends or the number of regulations it imposes, but by the confidence, enterprise and ingenuity of its people. It is built by those who take risks, start businesses, employ others, run shops, run pubs, manufacture goods and provide services. It is built from the ground up. Yet at precisely the moment when we should be strengthening the foundations of our economy, this Government are placing an ever greater pressure on the very businesses that sustain it. I fear that this Government simply do not understand the reality of running a business in Britain today. Indeed, we have seen that in the last couple of weeks. Take the comments by the Chief Secretary to the Treasury that employers are not working people. I do not think a political soundbite has resonated with so many across the country for a long time. I cannot overstate the hurt and insult that that comment caused to the men and women of this country who have had an idea, who get up early, who have gone out and built something, and who have given their employees a start in life, such as a young apprentice they have taken on, even if it means that they have to reduce their own pay to keep open or keep operating. They are the first ones out to work in the morning and the last ones home in the evening. Those comments hurt people, and although the Minister has apologised, I believe that she perfectly summed up the dire situation that this Government have caused for businesses up and down the country. At the autumn Budget in 2024, the then Chancellor announced an increase in employer national insurance contributions of 1.2 percentage points alongside a reduction in the threshold at which employers begin to pay national insurance from £9,100 to £5,000. That happened despite Labour having promised that it would not do it. Ultimately, businesses have three options: absorb the additional cost, pass it on to their customers through higher prices or reduce their costs elsewhere. Both the Centre for Policy Studies and the Office for Budget Responsibility warned that those measures would lead to higher consumer prices and lower nominal wages. They have affected 1.2 million employers, and 940,000 people have lost out financially. They leave the average employer facing a net increase that will see their liabilities rise by approximately £26,000. Those are not abstract figures; they represent real businesses, real jobs and real decisions about whether to invest, expand or even remain open. I want briefly to bring the debate closer to home by highlighting the experience of some local businesses in my constituency. Cherrywood Kitchen in Netley, run by Jason Hardcastle, is a small hospitality café that provides local employment and contributes to the community. He has seen a clear impact on the operating costs of his café since 2024, with national insurance contributions rising by over £2,000, VAT liabilities increasing by £4,000 and a weekly wage cost now exceeding £12,500. His cafe is busy. He has seen turnover increase every year that he has operated, but the actions of this Government have meant that he now takes on fewer people and does not take any profit home at the end of the week. Another local business owner, Matthew Boyle, operates a number of excellent hospitality venues in my constituency, employing local young people—people who the Government claim they want to support. He spent 23 years building his hospitality business, which now employs 175 people, but this Budget and this Government’s actions will add £230,000 of additional annual costs to his business.

My hon. Friend makes an important point. Is he struck, as I am when I meet these business people, by how physically broken they sometimes look because they simply do not know how they are going to survive? Their life’s work and their dreams have been torn to shreds by this Government.

My right hon. Friend makes an excellent point, and I go through the same thing as him. One of the most frustrating things on a Friday, when I go to see businesses in my area, is that I have no hope to give them because this Government have given them no hope. The Government need to listen to business people like Matthew who create the jobs and the wealth in the country that they love spending so much. Ministers must recognise that businesses are not simply a source of revenue for the Treasury; they are the wealth creators of our economy. That is why I am delighted that the Leader of the Opposition has set out our party’s policies on how we would help to meet the challenge that the Government have caused including, as my right hon. Friend the Member for Daventry (Stuart Andrew) said, by halving national insurance contributions for people aged 21 to 24, saving £1,500 for employers, and abolishing business rates for hospitality. I also believe that we need to consider a VAT cut for hospitality businesses. If we want thriving high streets, more jobs, better wages and a stronger economy, we must start by making Britain a better place to do business. Employers are working people because they create prosperity—not the Government, and certainly not this Government who are actively making the situation worse. It is not the Government who create prosperity; it is the people and businesses of this country, and they deserve better than what they are getting under this dire Labour Government.

Before I came to this House, I spent 17 years in the private sector as a chartered accountant, working with businesses in the food and drink, construction and utility sectors. I sat with owners as they went through their accounts, line by line, working out whether they could afford to take on one more person. When this House talks about business owners, I think of people who put their savings and even their own homes on the line so that others can earn a wage. There are a great many of them. At the start of 2025, there were 5.7 million private sector businesses in the country. Small and medium-sized firms provide almost 17 million jobs—almost three in five private sector jobs—and family firms sit at the heart of that, employing almost 14 million people in the country. The value of a successful business goes far beyond numbers. In my constituency of Mid Leicestershire, there is David North in Rothley, a family deli that has served the village for more than 50 years; Barrie Stephen in Anstey, a salon that started in one village and has trained stylists who went on to open businesses of their own; and S. J. Langton in The Square in Glenfield. Businesses like those give a teenager their first job and offer the apprenticeship that lets a young person build a career without leaving home. They are the shops that keep our villages alive, but how have this Government treated them? In the Government’s first Budget they raised employer national insurance contributions to 15% and cut the threshold to just £5,000. The accountancy firm UHY Hacker Young found that national insurance bills for employers rose by almost £28 billion in a single year. That is more than the Government’s own forecast. When we tax something more, we get less of it. Today, small firms planning to cut jobs outnumber those that are planning to hire by more than three to one. Then came the Employment Rights Act 2025, with new costs and new risks for every firm and every new hire. Then there were the business rates, and the results were entirely predictable. The Federation of Small Businesses confidence index fell to minus 71 at the end of last year. The business confidence monitor of the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales has now been negative for seven consecutive quarters. The headwinds are getting stronger. Inflation rose to 3.5% in September, with motor fuel up by almost 30% on the year. The OBR has cut growth forecasts for next year to just 1%, and last week the Bank of England raised interest rates for the first time in over three years. Small firms looked to last month’s Budget to help, but the verdict of the Federation of Small Businesses was blunt. Those firms got “nothing to ease sky-high energy bills, and nothing to make hiring someone more affordable.” Employer national insurance remains at 15%—the jobs tax remains. The Conservatives take a different view: Governments do not create growth, businesses do. Our job is to back businesses and then get out of their way. That is why we will scrap the family business tax and the family farm tax. We will introduce a permanent 100% business rates relief for retail, hospitality and leisure, cutting bills for a quarter of a million pubs, shops and high-street businesses. We will halve employer national insurance on jobs for those aged between 20 and 24, because the cost of giving a young person their first break has soared under this Government.

I will not. We would repeal Labour’s Employment Rights Act 2025, replace IR35, review Making Tax Digital, scrap the packaging tax and simplify tax for small businesses and the self-employed. I started working in my early teens, because if I wanted something, I had to earn it. This is the bargain that every business owner makes: they take the risk and do the work, and all they ask is that the Government do not stand in their way. Back them, and they will build this country. Tax them into retreat, and they will stop. The Government must decide which side they are on.

“Yes”—it is a small word, but it is absolutely crucial to creating a successful economy. Yes to that first investment; yes to opening that business; yes to giving that young person a job; yes to taking that risk; yes to expanding; yes to investing—all those things are so crucial to getting a successful company and a successful economy. However, the Government cannot build an economy by making it harder for businesses to say yes. The economy responds not to a Prime Minister saying, “We must have growth,” and his intentions, but to the incentives that Ministers put in place—or, in this case, the disincentives. We have heard it mentioned before—in relation to the jobs guarantee, for example—that the Government are trying to incentivise people into work, while at the same time disincentivising businesses from taking on people. That is like pressing the accelerator while putting on the handbrake. The Government have given so many businesses a reason to say no. The NICs increase, the business rates increase, the minimum wage increase and the red tape in the Employment Rights Act are a toxic concoction for our businesses, and are having a devastating effect. Let me take the examples of the café in Burbage, the restaurant in Barwell and Earl Shilton or even the gym in Hinckley. They have had the jobs tax. They have had the minimum wage go up. They have had employment red tape added. They have had business support changed and taken away. They have had business rates go up. They have had their energy bills go up—there was no support in the Budget for that. Is it any wonder that the ONS has said that from October 2026, some 16% fewer hospitality businesses have been created? Across the entire economy, business creation is down by 3.5%. Let us turn to the wider argument about the environment. As my constituency neighbour, my hon. Friend the Member for Mid Leicestershire (Mr Bedford), has said, business confidence has been down for seven consecutive negative quarters. Businesses are losing the confidence to say yes. Why? Because of the employment costs. In a report by the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales, 53% of businesses cite labour costs and 41% cite taxation. That figure is double what it used to be. Young people have been mentioned a lot. There are 981,000 people aged between 16 and 24 who are not in education, work or training. That is 30,000 more than last year. It is almost 1 million people, for the first time since 2013. That compares unfavourably with the likes of EU countries; for the first time ever, we are above the EU average. Why does all this matter? The contribution from my hon. Friend the Member for Hornchurch and Upminster (Julia Lopez) from the Opposition Front Bench got me thinking. We can count the trees that have fallen, but we cannot see the forest that has never been planted. What do I mean by that? We can see the 12,000 job losses in Poundland. We know that Morrisons has had to lay off 5,000 people. Jaguar Land Rover has had to lay off 4,000 people. Claire’s on the high street has had to lay off 2,500 people. Whitbread, which runs Premier Inn, has had to lay off 3,800 people. We can also count the young people who are going abroad. We know that 250,000 people went, of whom two thirds were under the age of 35. But what about the businesses that never opened? What about the investment that was never made, the job that was never offered, or the apprenticeship that was never started? The cost of this Labour Government’s “no” economy is so great. This is about the opportunity that has never been taken, and the future that we could have had. That is not recorded in any figures. No matter how hard this Government tell businesses to hire, they cannot force people to be hired, or force young people to stay. We cannot build a “yes” economy by giving businesses thousands of reasons to say no. That is why I support the motion.

It is a pleasure to take part in this debate, Madam Deputy Speaker. I started my business at the end of my first year at university. By my third year, it was paying me more than I thought any employer sensibly would—that is, if anyone would be foolish enough to take me on in the first place—so I carried on building that business, with no business experience and no knowledge of how to do anything. I had to learn everything from scratch. Lloyds became my business bankers, and although they were supportive, the sight of the black horse on an envelope was enough to make my palms sweat from sheer stress. All it takes is for the bank to withdraw its support, and your whole business—all your hours, hopes and dreams—are gone. The Minister is unusual in having some feeling for and understanding of private business. One of the problems is that Government Front Benchers in particular, and the parliamentary Labour party overall, do not. If you do not understand the dynamics of a business—the pressure and the reality of trying to build a business—you will not understand why people were outraged by the Chief Secretary to the Treasury’s remark about employers not being working people. That outrage is not fake; it is real and visceral. Their sense of disappointment in their Government is so strong. Many of them will have voted for this Government, based on their promise that growth would be the No. 1 thing, and that tax would not be put up. It sounded great in the manifesto. Those people feel betrayed by the lack of understanding and empathy for the fact that they are risking everything, including the home that they share with a spouse, who has to sign up as well. They have put all that on the line to create a business. That is the only way to create wealth. The state facilitates—through the rule of law, decent health services, education and the rest of it—but it does not deliver wealth. That can only come from the private sector, and that failure of understanding and personal experience has led to this desperate situation. The previous Chancellor, the right hon. Member for Leeds West and Pudsey (Rachel Reeves), made a manifesto pledge that must have been made because some public relations person told Labour, the weekend before the election, that if it did not make that pledge, it might not win, and not to be complacent: “Let’s promise not to put tax up on working people.” The Government then broke that pledge by coming up with the clever wheeze of putting tax up on employers, with no understanding of what that would do. The arithmetic is really depressing. The £26 billion hit to the economy meant that there was not £26 billion to spend on the NHS. It turned out that the increase did not even raise the £16 billion that, according to the OBR, it should have, once the cut in corporation profits and so on was accounted for. The Government then had to compensate the public sector, which brought the figure down to £11 billion or £10 billion. Then they said, “Oh, no, hospices and GPs are not technically part of this,” so they had to find more money. Single-digit billions is all that the Government got for putting a £26 billion or £27 billion brake on the economy. It is utterly insane. It is noticeable that smaller and smaller numbers of Labour MPs want to come to the Chamber to defend that decision. I congratulate those who have, on their party loyalty if nothing else, but when I talk to Labour colleagues outside this Chamber—if I have a chat with them in the bar, for example—I struggle to find any Labour MP who says, “That was a really good idea. That was the best way of raising money.” They will defend the need to raise money to stick into the health service, repair the “dreadful 14 years” and so on. They buy into that still, but they do not think that putting tax up on employers was a clever way of raising money, because it did not raise very much, it was an enormous brake on the economy, and it has been devastating. It has been most devastating

If the hon. Gentleman wants to intervene on me, I would be delighted to let him come in. Yesterday, the deputy governor of the Bank of England said that one of the reasons why youth unemployment has gone up faster than unemployment generally—remember, because of that gigantic brake on the economy, overall unemployment has gone up by 250,000 under this Government—was the cost of employing young people, including because of the minimum wage, the jobs tax and so on.
Would my right hon. Friend care to comment on the state of the graduate market, too?

The situation is affecting all young people, is it not? I have used this quote in the Chamber before, but it is worth repeating, even for the tiny number of Labour MPs who were prepared to come here, to vaguely try to support the Government. Ronald Reagan said about the left: “If it moves, tax it. If it keeps moving, regulate it. And if it stops moving, subsidise it.” Labour taxed it with a jobs tax; then it regulated it with the Employment Rights Act 2025 until it stopped moving. Then young people were not getting employed anymore. Labour said, “Yippee!” Labour MPs were literally going around the TV studios saying, “Look at us—there is a jobs guarantee.” They have taxed it; they have regulated it until no one is getting employed; and now they will say, “We will subsidise it.” They have absolutely no conception of how private enterprise works, or how the economy works. They are letting the country down, and they increasingly know it, albeit that they do not say so in the Chamber quite yet.

Two weeks ago, when I spoke in the Budget debate, I criticised the Government for deliberately increasing the cost of running a business and of hiring people, in the full knowledge that it would cause more unemployment. I said that it is constituents, including mine, who are paying the price for Labour’s economic failure with their jobs. What I did not realise at the time was quite how prescient those comments were. On Monday, one of the largest employers in my constituency, Kanes Foods, went into administration, with the loss of 662 jobs. That is 662 people who last week were paying national insurance and income tax, but who this week are on benefits. My thoughts are with every one of those employees and their families. Many people may not know or have heard of Kanes Foods, but most of us will have consumed its packaged salads or stir fries, which were on sale in major supermarkets and especially in Asda. Let me be clear that the business had some difficulties, and the administrators have particularly highlighted challenges with a recent waste water treatment issue. Let us be in no doubt, however, that Government policies did not help. When margins are as tight as they are in food production and distribution, even a tiny increase in labour costs can turn a profitable business into a loss-making one. When the Government whacked up the national living wage by way more than inflation, they added to businesses’ costs. When the Government increased employer national insurance, it added somewhere in the region of £700 or £800 to the cost of employing each and every worker. When a business has hundreds of employees, as Kanes did, that is hundreds of thousands of pounds of additional costs. When the Minister comes to the Dispatch Box in a few minutes’ time, I would like to see him at least acknowledge that the Government have played a part in large numbers of my constituents now being unemployed, and perhaps bring himself to say sorry. I hold the Government at least in part responsible for the situation, but on a more positive note, I thank the local community for supporting those impacted by the closure of Kanes Foods. In particular, I thank Primafruit, which has already gone out of its way to offer jobs to some of those who lost their jobs, and other businesses are coming forward. I also thank Jobcentre Plus in Evesham, which I spoke to yesterday, which is providing support for impacted constituents and information on how they can claim for pay, holiday pay and redundancy pay. The administrators are also working on that. I am also concerned about the knock-on impact on the supply chain—on suppliers to Kanes, and on those who are owed money by Kanes. I appeal to them to talk to the administrators. I am hopeful, as are the administrators, that somebody will come forward and buy some of Kanes’ business, or its site. We may be able to get something back and resurrect the business—once a vibrant local family business, right in the heart of the vale of Evesham—in some way, shape or form. A broader issue, and a key theme in today’s debate, is that this Government simply do not respect people who run their own businesses. They do not consider them to be workers, and the Government overall do not seem to have respect for the private sector. They do not seem to get business. They do not understand basic things like cash flow. They do not have a grasp of even the most basic economic principles, but that is not a surprise; they are socialists. As the saying goes, if a socialist understood economics, they would not be a socialist. Before entering Parliament, I spent 23 years in the private sector, and that amounts to more private sector experience than the Prime Minister, the Chancellor, the Business Secretary, the Home Secretary, the Foreign Secretary and the Housing Secretary have combined. In fact, it amounts to more private sector experience than is in 90% of the Cabinet, which is startling, but it probably goes some way to explaining why t

Nothing highlights the fiscal failure of this Government more starkly than the plight of Poundland. The chain’s 600 stores and 12,000 workers sit on the verge of collapse, not because customers have walked away—they have not; sales grew by 6.7% in September—but because of the Government’s unaffordable tax rises, which make it impossible to run a business that works on slim profit margins. Those that work on slim profit margins keep prices down for customers. How ironic it is that a Government who preach about helping the least well-off and helping with the cost of living are forcing those firms out of business. Business owners in my constituency are mystified by the damage that the Government have inflicted on businesses up and down the country. What I am asked by them most often is, “Do this Government not understand the harm that they are doing, or is it that they just do not care?” They have concluded that it is both. The Chief Secretary to the Treasury, the right hon. Member for Wycombe (Emma Reynolds), made sure of that when she said that employers were not working people—which, by the way, was a kick in the teeth for every employer in the country who is often at work before everyone else, and leaves work after everyone else. When the former Chancellor, the right hon. Member for Leeds West and Pudsey (Rachel Reeves), announced that she would raise business and employer-related taxes by over £50 billion by the end of the decade, she wanted money for Labour’s pet projects—benefits and net zero—and she did not care that they squeezed the life out of businesses. Labour did not care where that money came from. I asked the right hon. Lady on several occasions whether she expected the number of jobs to go up or down when she taxed them. She did not say. She did not know. She was shocked. Labour does not seem to understand that you cannot tax your way to growth and you cannot spend your way out of debt. The consequences have been job losses and, combined with day one workers’ rights, fewer opportunities. The tax rate policy hit on family businesses was hard as well.

I have sat here for nearly an hour and a half, and I have not heard anything from Conservative Members about how they will address the elephant in the room: how to generate economic growth and rebuild trade relationships with our closest partners in the EU and elsewhere. Instead, we just hear criticism of the national insurance jobs tax. I completely agree with the right hon. Lady about that, but we are not hearing anything—
Order. This is a debate about employers, not about our relationship with the EU.

When it comes to getting costs down for employers, I would start with energy. I welcome the Government’s—eventually—approving the drilling in Jackdaw, and they need to admit to doing the same in Rosebank and going further. They should look at what our neighbours in Norway have managed to do by drilling in their country. Let me return to the subject of family businesses. The Government showed a complete lack of knowledge of family businesses and how they are run when they capped what would have been 100% tax relief for business properties and taxed the assets as they did so. They did not understand that the life of a business can be a couple of years—it may not last—or it can go on for generations. It does not end when the founder of the business dies; it goes on. The Government did not seem to have a clue about that; they showed complete disregard. The other thing my constituents talk about is why the Government hate wealth creators. Why do they hate the wealthy? It must be—has to be—the politics of envy and jealousy. Frankie Dyer of Barbakan Delicatessen—one company in my constituency, but it could have be any of the 365 hospitality businesses there—sent an open letter to the Prime Minister before the Budget. She wanted help, particularly with national insurance contributions, which have had the worst impacts on her business, now costing her an extra £1,000 per employee. If someone has 50 or more employees, they will have no profit left at all, and they certainly cannot invest to grow their business. Frankie said that her business is second-generation, and it is 62 years old. It is now facing severe financial pressures. Despite the business having an annual turnover exceeding £2.3 million and winning more than 10 awards for its products, soaring operational costs—energy bills, tax obligations and national insurance—mean that the business is now struggling to stay afloat and to pay its bills each week.
